items.description: Οι τραυματικοί μυϊκοί τραυματισμοί, είτε από τραύματα στο πεδίο της μάχης, πυροβολισμούς, χειρουργικές εκτομές ή μεγάλα ανοιχτά κατάγματα, μπορούν να προκαλέσουν ογκομετρική μυϊκή απώλεια (VML), την απώλεια τόσο πολύ ιστού που ο μυς δεν μπορεί να αναγεννηθεί μόνος του. Η ανάρρωση συνήθως φέρνει χρόνια φλεγμονή, ουλές και μόνιμη αδυναμία. Οι τρέχουσες θεραπείες παραμένουν παρηγορητικές, w…
items.descriptionOriginal: Traumatic muscle injuries, whether from battlefield wounds, gunshots, surgical resections, or major open fractures, can cause volumetric muscle loss (VML), the loss of so much tissue that the muscle cannot regenerate on its own. Recovery typically brings chronic inflammation, scarring, and permanent weakness. Current treatments remain palliative, with none reliably restoring the lost muscle.

items.description: Τα αεροπορικά ταξίδια δεν πηγαίνουν πάντα όπως τα σχεδιάζετε. Αυτό ίσχυε ιδιαίτερα το περασμένο Σαββατοκύριακο, καθώς η FAA καθήλωσε άνευ προηγουμένου χιλιάδες αεροπλάνα, ακυρώνοντας και καθυστερώντας πτήσεις και προκαλώντας πραγματικά όλεθρο στους ταξιδιώτες. Οι λόγοι πίσω από το κλείσιμο εξακολουθούν να διευκρινίζονται στα παρασκήνια. Αλλά αυτή η ιστορία δεν αφορά αυτό. Αντίθετα, είναι η ιστορία…
items.descriptionOriginal: Air travel doesn’t always go as planned. That was especially true this past weekend, as the FAA unprecedentedly grounded thousands of planes, canceling and delaying flights and genuinely wreaking havoc on travelers. The reasons behind the shutdown are still being sorted out behind the scenes. But this story isn’t about that. Instead, it’s the tale of what could have been an extremely negative situation and how the butterfly effect changed lives. This was the case for at least two travelers, who turned the lemon-like circumstance into the refreshing start of a new friendship. An Instagram video posted by NBC LA News begins with a blonde woman making a bold statement: “I don’t want to say that the universe shut down aviation just so Michelle and I could become friends,” she declares. A chyron over the clip reads, “A friendship takes flight after the FAA ground stop.” View this post on Instagram Things started to get weird NBC LA Journalist Karma Dickerson explains, “Nikki Chambers was waiting to board her flight from El Paso Friday afternoon, when things started to get weird.” The clip bounces back to Chambers, who shares how odd things had begun to get at the airport. “And it even said ‘flight left’ on the screen, and I’m like, ‘No, it didn’t! We’re still here.’” She laughs and rolls her eyes. “So it seemed really eerie.” Dickerson continues, “Michelle Navarro was sitting nearby, noting the same.” We then see Navarro, who’s listed only as “traveler,” share with the news outlet how it all went down. “There was an influx of law enforcement and dogs. And they were running the dogs,” she explained. The two women got to chatting The two women began chatting, Dickerson explains. Chambers continues, “I go, ‘Where do you live?’ She said Westminster. And I’m like, ‘I’m in Huntington!’” Quite some time later, they made a decision. Dickerson shares, “Four hours into the nationwide ground stop and their in-depth convo, they called it. It was time for a new plan. With all the uncertainty, Nikki felt safer on the ground. And Michelle? She had somewhere to be.” Navarro then reveals that that day was actually quite special. She tells Dickerson, “Today was my wedding shower!” We then flash to a photo of Navarro surrounded by friends at a restaurant wearing a wedding veil. Dickerson laughs, reporting, “As you might have guessed, she made it. Thanks to a 12-hour car ride with a stranger.” Navarro jokes, “She didn’t look like a serial killer, so I was like, ‘Alright, let’s do this!’” A decision based on snacks The video cuts back to Chambers, who explains what ultimately led her to trust her new friend. “She pulled out this little tray of snacks that her fiancé had made for her, with all kinds of little nibblies in it. And she offered me some. And at that moment, I’m like, I’m getting in a van with this lady, aren’t I? She’s got good snacks!” We then see a photo of two women making peace signs in comfy clothes as they embark on their road adventure. The reporter relays, “So the two Orange County women set out at 7:00 a.m., their rented car upgraded to a minivan, turning what could have been a brutal 800-mile trek into an impromptu great American road trip.” Wedding plans Chambers explains, “By about mid-trip, she’s like, ‘Do you want to come to the wedding?’” She covers her mouth and then flashes a huge smile. “I’m like, ‘Yes!’” Wrapping up the story, Dickerson shares, “So at the very least, we know Michelle and Nikki will be meeting again once more. Though both women tell me they suspect that, as they embark on their next life adventures, they’ll be doing it with a new friend along for the ride.” The story delighted many Instagrammers and inspired them, too. One writes, “Next, you will find them using this in their airline campaigns. ‘Flight canceled? Hang out in one of our restaurants and make a friend.’” Another points out that this is a sure sign that adults can make friends as easily as we did in childhood. “So often we lament it’s too bad we can’t just make friends as easily as we did in kindergarten and here these women are, proving it’s still possible to get by on proximity, vibes, and snacks.” Yet another shares what many Gen Xers might have been thinking: “It’s giving Planes, Trains, and Automobiles lol, convenient movie for the holiday month.” The post Two strangers stranded at El Paso airport take epic leap of faith in 12-hour road trip together appeared first on Upworthy .

items.titleOriginal: A man found a 2-hour-old baby in a London phone box in 1994. Now she’s raising money so he can retire.
items.description: Τις πρώτες πρωινές ώρες της 30ης Απριλίου 1994, ο Joe Campbell πήγε στον τηλεφωνικό θάλαμο κοντά στο σπίτι του στο Forest Gate, στο Ανατολικό Λονδίνο, για να τηλεφωνήσει στους γονείς του στη Γουιάνα. Στην αρχή, σκέφτηκε ότι υπήρχε μια πεταμένη σακούλα με πατατάκια μέσα. Ήταν ένα νεογέννητο κορίτσι, περίπου δύο ωρών, με τον ομφάλιο λώρο του ακόμα συνδεδεμένο. Ο Κάμπελ κάλεσε το 999 (η βρετανική έκδοση του 911) α…
items.descriptionOriginal: In the early hours of April 30, 1994, Joe Campbell walked to the phone booth near his home in Forest Gate, East London , to call his parents in Guyana. At first, he thought there was a discarded bag of chips inside. It was a newborn girl, about two hours old, with her umbilical cord still attached. Campbell called 999 (the British version of 911) and stayed with her until help arrived. He asked if he could adopt her, but he was told no, in part because he wasn’t married. But he gave her the name “April,” and for years he sent her birthday cards and presents until social services eventually asked him to stop. She was adopted by another family when she was 3. She grew up knowing almost nothing about the man who found her until 2016, at age 22, she made a public appeal in the London newspaper Metro to find him. A colleague at the delivery company where Campbell worked saw it and showed him. View this post on Instagram “I ran home and [told] my daughter Rihanna on the phone, ‘I think I found April,’” Campbell recalled on Good Morning Britain . They reunited that summer, and they’ve been family ever since. She changed her name to April, and she calls him Dad. View this post on Instagram “Joe is complete family,” she said, according to SWNS . “His kids are my siblings now. We’re so close, we stay at each other’s houses. He never stopped thinking about me. I don’t know what this man is. An angel.” Campbell is now 62 and still drives a bus. So April, a bank employee in West London, has started a fundraiser to help him retire early. The pair went back on Good Morning Britain in October to talk about the decade since their reunion. The post A man found a 2-hour-old baby in a London phone box in 1994. Now she’s raising money so he can retire. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.title: Οι Βρετανοί παππούδες δοκιμάζουν για πρώτη φορά το «Minnesota sushi», το «puppy chow» και άλλα κλασικά Midwestern
items.titleOriginal: British grandparents taste ‘Minnesota sushi,’ ‘puppy chow,’ and other Midwestern classics for the first time
items.description: Στο κανάλι τους στο JOLLY YouTube, οι δημιουργοί περιεχομένου Josh και Ollie κάνουν κάθε είδους διασκεδαστικά πειράματα πολιτιστικής σύγκρουσης με φαγητό . Πρόσφατα αποφάσισαν να δουν τι θα έφτιαχναν οι Βρετανοί παππούδες, ή «αποφυγές του φέρετρου», όπως περιέγραψαν τους εαυτούς τους, από κάποιο κλασικό φαγητό της Midwestern. Η μεσοδυτική κουζίνα τείνει να ευνοεί το χορταστικό, χορταστικό φαγητό με άφθονο…
items.descriptionOriginal: On their JOLLY YouTube channel, content creators Josh and Ollie do all kinds of fun culture-clash experiments featuring food . They recently decided to see what British grandparents, or “coffin dodgers,” as they described themselves, would make of some classic Midwestern comfort food. Midwestern cuisine tends to favor hearty, filling food with plenty of casseroles (also known as hotdishes), creamy sauces, and generous helpings of meat, cheese, and potatoes. Much of the region’s food traditions were shaped by European immigrants, particularly Germans and Scandinavians, as well as the ingredients and practical cooking styles that became common across the Midwest. That might sound pretty familiar to a British palate. British cuisine has its own long history of hearty meals built around meat, potatoes, vegetables, gravy, and other comforting staples. But familiar ingredients don’t always make for familiar dishes. These grandparents’ reactions prove just how much room there is for cultural confusion at the dinner table. First up were the appetizers, which included ranch dressing with vegetables, cheese curds, and “Minnesota sushi” Thanks to the World Cup , many non-Americans were introduced to ranch and became instantly obsessed, with some even trying to smuggle or ship it back home. This time around, the condiment was equally well received. The grandparents described it as “ubiquitous” and “cheeky but not flippant,” which is both hilarious and, somehow, a pretty good description of ranch. “Minnesota sushi,” on the other hand, required a little more explanation. Despite its name, it contains no fish, rice, or seaweed. Instead, softened cream cheese and a pickle are rolled up in deli meat and sliced into little pinwheels. The grandparents weren’t quite as enthusiastic about this one, though it earned praise for its “nice crunch” and for being “non-threatening.” Cheese curds were another story. Josh and Ollie dubbed them “prepubescent cheese,” referring to the fact that cheese curds are the solid chunks of milk that eventually become cheese. Despite the slightly alarming name, they went over pretty well. Moving on to the main course: meatloaf, taco salad, and tater tot casserole Meatloaf got off to a slightly rocky start when it was compared to an elephant’s foot and even the radioactive runoff from the Chernobyl disaster. But apparently, appearances weren’t everything. Despite the unflattering comparisons, the grandparents declared it “delicious” and “proper English men’s food.” Tater tot casserole, more often called hotdishes among Midwesterners, is often made with a layer of seasoned ground meat, some veggies, and melted cheese. And of course, a crowning layer of crispy tater tots. This was a bit of a two-for-one discovery, as the hosts had to first explain what a tater tot was. A typical tater tot casserole. Photo credit: Canva The taco salad was also a hit, even if they did pronounce it “tah-co” salad. This dish has an interesting American history, too. According to The New York Times , the taco salad got its start at Disneyland’s Casa de Fritos restaurant in 1955, where staff created an edible corn-chip cup called the “Ta-Cup.” Finally, dessert: if peanut butter can be added, peanut butter will be added As one viewer put it, “The thing about the Midwest is, if we can slap peanut butter into a dessert, by thunder we will.” The desserts in question were Puppy Chow (also known as Muddy Buddies), made with crispy cereal coated in melted chocolate and peanut butter and tossed in powdered sugar, and Scotcheroos, which combines a chewy peanut butter-and-crispy rice-cereal base with melted chocolate and butterscotch. A bowl of Puppy Chow. Photo credit: Canva And to wash it all down, the Brits had Faygo and root beer The grandparents found Faygo “too sweet” and “undrinkable,” and root beer seemed to taste medicinal. That can be chalked up to its distinctive wintergreen flavor, which is used in many mouthwashes, dental rinses, and toothpastes in Britain. For the most part, the grandparents seemed to enjoy their tour through Midwestern cuisine. Some dishes earned immediate approval, while others required a little more convincing. But the food wasn’t quite the best part of the video. At the end, Josh and Ollie asked their taste testers to share a little life advice. The grandparents offered wonderfully simple answers. Here are some of the best nuggets: “Have lots of fun.” “Make the most of every day.” “Don’t take yourself too seriously.” “Be kind and love people.” “Whatever dream you have, go for it.” “Never stop learning.” While we may have different opinions on root beer and “prepubescent cheese,” we can agree on their advice, no matter which side of the pond we hail from. Follow JOLLY on YouTube for even more delicious and delightful food reviews. The post British grandparents taste ‘Minnesota sushi,’ ‘puppy chow,’ and other Midwestern classics for the first time appeared first on Upworthy .

items.title: Μια μελέτη με παιδιά της δεκαετίας του '90 διαπίστωσε ότι τα τακτικά ταξίδια στο πάρκο συνδέονται με 17% καλύτερη ψυχική υγεία
items.titleOriginal: A study of ’90s kids found that regular trips to the park are linked to 17 percent better mental health
items.description: Δεν είναι μυστικό ότι τα smartphone, το YouTube και τα iPad έχουν αλλάξει δραματικά την παιδική ηλικία για τα Gen Z και Gen Alpha. Από τότε που εμφανίστηκαν τα smartphone και τα iPad, τα παιδιά πέρασαν πολύ λιγότερο χρόνο σε εξωτερικούς χώρους. Το 2009, το 7% των παιδιών ηλικίας 6 έως 17 ετών πέρασαν μία ώρα ή λιγότερο στη φύση. Το 2025, ο αριθμός αυτός έχει υπερτετραπλασιαστεί σε 26%. Ένα νέο καρφί…
items.descriptionOriginal: It’s no secret that smartphones, YouTube, and iPads have dramatically changed what childhood looks like for Gen Z and Gen Alpha. Since smartphones and iPads came on the scene, kids have spent far less time outdoors. In 2009, 7% of children ages 6 to 17 spent an hour or less in nature. In 2025, that number has more than quadrupled to 26%. A new study from the University of Exeter shows why it’s so important for kids to spend plenty of time outside, especially when they’re playing with others. Researchers found that children who grew up in the ‘90s and visited a park at least once a week scored 16.5% better on mental health assessments than those who did not. Kids running on the playground. Photo credit: Canva The study used data from the Children of the 90s long-term cohort study. The study recruited more than 14,000 pregnant women from April 1991 to December 1992 and followed their children extensively for decades. Taking children to parks is great for their mental health “Our research suggests encouraging children to visit parks and playgrounds at least once a week could be a practical way to support their emotional wellbeing, social skills and mental health. But for this to work fairly, communities need good-quality parks that are safe, accessible and welcoming to families from all backgrounds,” lead researcher Mark Ferguson of the University of Exeter said in a statement . “Parks give children space to be physically active, which is known to support mental and physical health, as well as helping adventurous and imaginative play to build confidence and independence. We believe parks could be more than places to play, but an important resource for children’s healthy development,” Ferguson continued. Play equipment from the ’90s. Photo credit: Canva The study comes at a time when there has been a sharp increase in mental health disorders among children and teens. According to the 2026 Health of Women and Children Report , nearly 12.4 million American children had a diagnosed mental health condition in 2023- 2024, approximately 3 million more than in 2016-2017. Parks are a great place for strengthening mental health When children spend time at a park, they learn to make new friends, persevere through a tough run on the monkey bars, and use their imaginations. This supports their social-emotional development and helps them handle everyday challenges. Building a strong foundation of social-emotional development lays the groundwork for good mental health in childhood and beyond. A young girl with an iPad. Photo credit: Canva The researchers also found an interesting tidbit about children’s socioeconomic backgrounds. Young children born into more affluent families spend more time in parks than socioeconomically disadvantaged children. But as they get older, the pattern shifts: advantaged children go to the park less than disadvantaged children. The study is a great reminder of how important it is for kids to get out and play at their local parks. It’s also a call for communities to set aside ample space for parks and recreation areas and ensure they are safe and well staffed. As the study shows, going to the park isn’t just about an afternoon of fun for a child, but a lifetime of improved mental health. The post A study of ’90s kids found that regular trips to the park are linked to 17 percent better mental health appeared first on Upworthy .

items.title: Κλέφτες έκλεψαν τον εξοπλισμό της επιχείρησης περιποίησης γκαζόν 14χρονης. Ευγενικοί άγνωστοι πρόσφεραν 37.000 δολάρια για να βοηθήσουν.
items.titleOriginal: Thieves stole 14-year-old’s lawn care business equipment. Kind strangers donated $37,000 to help.
items.description: Ο Sonny Gallardo, 14, και η οικογένειά του βγήκαν έξω από το χωριό Prairie Village του Κάνσας, το σπίτι τους το Halloween σε μια συγκλονιστική ανακάλυψη: ο πολύτιμος (και ακριβός) εξοπλισμός περιποίησης του γκαζόν του είχε κλαπεί μέσα σε μια νύχτα. "Ξύπνησα και η γιαγιά μου είπε ότι μας έκλεψαν τον εξοπλισμό. Βγήκα έξω και είχε [φύγει]", λέει ο Gallardo στο Upworthy. «Δεν το πίστευα στην αρχή.…
items.descriptionOriginal: Sonny Gallardo, 14, and his family stepped outside their Prairie Village, Kansas, home on Halloween to a shocking discovery: his precious (and pricey) lawn care equipment had been stolen overnight. “I woke up, and my grandma said our equipment got stolen. I walked outside, and it was [gone],” Gallardo tells Upworthy. “I didn’t believe it at first. I still don’t. We assumed it was safe.” The ninth-grader and his family, who founded his lawn-mowing and lawn-care business named Sunnyside Jobs, LLC, went to the police station to file a report. What happened next has left them shocked, humbled, and grateful. View this post on Instagram Gallardo’s lawn care business beginnings Gallardo started mowing lawns when he was just 10 years old. “I know how it feels to walk outside to a nice lawn,” he tells Upworthy. “It brings other people joy.” With the help of his grandma Monica, his grandpa, two friends, and his aunt (who handles administrative work), the business expanded to offer power washing, leaf and junk removal, and more. “We do everything,” Gallardo adds. “It’s fun. I just really like doing it. It’s satisfying to me, and [we mow] about 30-35 lawns.” So when his equipment—including a 10-foot trailer with five lawn mowers on it, totaling over $20,000—was stolen, he was devastated. Until his community and kind strangers rallied around him. Donations flood in for Gallardo Gallardo’s grandmother started a GoFundMe to help cover the costs of the arduous process of buying back his lawn-care equipment. “They also cleared out everything from the back of the work vehicle,” she wrote. “Everything Sonny has worked so hard for was gone in minutes. Sonny was completely devastated, and so is the family.” Unfortunately, Gallardo was in the process of securing insurance for his newly formed LLC—but “coverage was not yet in place.” Within the first day or two, they raised about $600 toward a $20,000 goal. That’s when a local Kansas City news station learned about Gallardo’s situation. With their coverage, the GoFundMe goal was exceeded within weeks. Today, kind strangers have donated nearly $35,000 to help re-establish his business. “It’s crazy. It’s been a lot of support, especially from the lawn mowing community,” Gallardo tells Upworthy. “They’ve donated a lot of lawn equipment. I’m still doing lawns and leaf pickup.” His grandmother credits Sonny with being fiscally responsible, noting that he had enough saved to buy a new lawn mower in the interim. “We’ve been receiving all of these blessings. It’s overwhelming,” she tells Upworthy. With the funds, Gallardo plans to grow his business. “We’re for sure going to expand and have more crews out there,” he shared. Nearly 900 people have donated and left hopeful, personal notes for Gallardo and his family. “You’re inspiring young man, and don’t lose heart from this setback. Keep your spirits up!” one wrote. Another added, “You are an inspirational and determined young man, you will always succeed with such attributes. Peace & blessings.” The post Thieves stole 14-year-old’s lawn care business equipment. Kind strangers donated $37,000 to help. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.title: Feel-Good τηλεοπτικά αγαπημένα: 30 σειρές ροής που θα φωτίσουν την ημέρα σας
items.titleOriginal: Feel-Good TV Favorites: 30 Streaming Shows That’ll Brighten Your Day
items.description: Ποια είναι η συνταγή για μια καλή τηλεοπτική εκπομπή; Για κάποιους, είναι ένας συνδυασμός ρομαντισμού και χιούμορ. Για άλλους, είναι μια νοσταλγική ιστορία με συγγενείς χαρακτήρες. Και μερικές φορές συμβαίνει ακριβώς το αντίθετο: ριάλιτι απόδρασης που σε μεταφέρει κάπου μακριά. Ευτυχώς, οι ενθουσιώδεις ιστορίες όλων των ειδών είναι διαθέσιμες για ροή όλες τις ώρες της ημέρας (και της νύχτας).…
items.descriptionOriginal: What’s the recipe for a feel-good TV show? For some, it’s a mix of romance and humor. For others, it’s a nostalgic storyline with relatable characters. And sometimes it’s just the opposite: escapism reality TV that transports you somewhere far away. Luckily, uplifting stories of all kinds are available to stream at all hours of the day (and night). From comedies and coming-of-age-stories to heartwarming reality series, these shows can help you feel a little better about the world. So, make yourself a cup of tea and cozy up on the couch — a heartwarming streaming session awaits! A Man on the Inside | Netflix This is perhaps the most wholesome whodunit you’ll ever watch. In Season One, retired professor Charles (Ted Danson) goes undercover at a retirement community to investigate the theft of a family heirloom. The next season, he takes on a new case at a college campus where he meets Mona, played by Danson’s real-life wife of over 30 years, Mary Steenburgen. We’re excited to see what’s in store for Season Three, which, alas, will be this endearing tale’s final chapter . Abbott Elementary | Hulu This hilarious mockumentary series follows teachers (and an outrageous principal) at a Philadelphia public school who go above and beyond to help their students succeed, despite the hurdles the faculty encounters both in and out of the classroom. Fun fact: Abbott Elementary is named after Joyce Abbott , a real sixth-grade teacher who taught creator and star Quinta Brunson at Andrew Hamilton School in Philadelphia. All Creatures Great and Small | PBS and Prime Video All Creatures Great and Small is based on author and veterinarian James Herriot’s beloved memoirs about his years treating animals in rural Yorkshire beginning in the 1930s. The British series is so peaceful that all six seasons feel like taking a breath of fresh air (the seventh premieres in the U.S. in January 2027). Black-ish | Hulu This Emmy-winning comedy is heartwarming, family-centered, and will keep you laughing. Follow the beloved Johnsons for eight seasons as they navigate highs, lows, and life changes together. Choir | Disney+ Meet the inspiring kids who make up the Detroit Youth Choir (of America’s Got Talent fame ) in this moving Disney+ docuseries. Over six episodes, you’ll find yourself cheering on all of the talented singers as they pursue their dreams and prepare for “the performance of a lifetime”: taking the stage at Carnegie Hall in New York City. Derry Girls | Netflix Witty and wonderful, Derry Girls is a British teen sitcom that follows a tight-knit group of friends during “ The Troubles ” in Ireland. It’s a beautiful example of the power of embracing humor amid hardships, without glossing over truths. English Teacher | Hulu English Teacher is another warmhearted, witty comedy set in the classroom, and often the faculty lounge and principal’s office as well. You’ll follow a group of offbeat high school teachers in Austin, Texas, as they navigate everything from a chaotic camping trip to AI-powered trash cans. The show boasts a rating of 94% on Rotten Tomatoes, and our only complaint is that the episodes, which run just over 20 minutes, aren’t longer — because the characters are endlessly fun to be around. Extraordinary Attorney Woo | Netflix South Korean series Extraordinary Attorney Woo follows a young lawyer who is on the autism spectrum as she navigates everyday interactions in her unique and authentic way. The show, which is dubbed in English, has a 93% audience score on Rotten Tomatoes and was the most-viewed title on Netflix for a week . Gilmore Girls | Hulu For a dose of mother-daughter love, Gilmore Girls offers seven seasons (and a four-part reunion series) of feel-good content. The young mom and her teenage daughter — played by Lauren Graham and Alexis Bledel, respectively — talk fast, drink a lot of coffee, and lean on each other through family drama, job changes, and romantic ups and downs. Hart of Dixie | HBO Max If you’re a fan of Gilmore Girls , this wholesome show will be right up your alley. Rachel Bilson stars as Zoe Hart, a doctor from New York City who inherits half of a family practice in the small, fictional town of Bluebell, Alabama: a perfectly cozy community where neighbors support each other, get tangled up in romance, and attend many a quirky festival. Home for Christmas | Netflix The first season of this Norwegian show follows Johanne, a 30-year-old single nurse, as she gives herself 24 days to find a boyfriend to bring home for Christmas. Three seasons later, the show (always set during the holidays) remains full of tender moments about navigating romance, independence, and family expectations. Is It Cake? | Netflix The premise is super simple and super silly: Contestants bake elaborate cakes that look like everyday items, including purses, paintings, and rubber ducks. The desserts are then placed next to the real objects they resemble, and guest judges have to guess which one is the cake. It’s fun to play along, though it’s delightfully tricky! Love on the Spectrum U.S. | Netflix There are plenty of reality shows about finding love, but Love on the Spectrum stands out — not only because its stars are neurodivergent but also because it possesses a warmth and hopefulness that make you truly root for the cast as they seek meaningful relationships. The U.S. version is a spinoff of the Australian series , and both are available to stream on Netflix. North of North | Netflix If you need a reminder that good things can come during uncertain times, this show fits the bill. Set in the tiny, fictional Arctic community of Ice Cove, North of North follows a young Inuk mother as she embarks on a new chapter after leaving her marriage. Viewers follow along with her highs and lows as she tries to get a handle on dating and building a career, while breaking down traditional gender expectations. Psych | Prime Video and Peacock Watch a quick-witted and perceptive police consultant (played by James Roday Rodriguez) solve cases using the power of observation — and the help of his reluctant BFF (played by Dulé Hill). The eight-season show combines comedy, drama, and detective work, all the while highlighting the infectious friendship between the two main characters. Tip: Keep an eye out for pineapples ! Queer Eye | Netflix The “Fab Five” gives emotional makeovers to ordinary folks across the country. But they don’t focus on appearance alone: The team explores the powerful connection between how we look, how we treat ourselves, and how we interact with the world — a reminder we can all use. Schitt’s Creek | Hulu Riches-to-rags is the premise of Schitt’s Creek : a series about a wealthy family who loses all their money and moves into a motel in a (very) small town. Laugh-out-loud moments, endearing friendships, and perfectly quotable one-liners earned this rewatchable, lighthearted show an Emmy for outstanding comedy in 2020. Shrinking | Apple TV On paper, Shrinking doesn’t sound particularly feel-good — it follows a father (played by Jason Segel) navigating parenthood and his career as a therapist following his wife’s sudden death. However, the show portrays grief through a lens that’s undeniably uplifting. It’s impossible not to fall in love with the nosy neighbors and hilarious coworkers, especially Paul, the lovably gruff mentor played by Harrison Ford (who earned his first Emmy nomination for the role at age 83). Sister, Sister | Paramount Plus A ’90s classic, Sister, Sister — starring twins Tia and Tamera Mowry — is still a joy to watch decades after it originally aired. Equally heart-filling and funny, the six-season series captures the magic of sisterhood and the positive impact of supportive family units. Somebody Feed Phil | Netflix There are many foodie travel shows out there, but this one has Phil Rosenthal. The creator of Everybody Loves Raymond supplies just the right amount of wholesome dad jokes as he tries local cuisine in Kyoto, Copenhagen, and Cape Town, among dozens of other cities around the world. All eight seasons are packed with enticing eats and conversations, but we’re partial to the first two, which include scenes of Rosenthal video chatting with his mom and dad before they passed away in 2019 and 2021, respectively. Somebody Somewhere | Prime Video Described as “a totally platonic love story” by HBO, Somebody Somewhere is about two coworkers (played by Bridget Everett and Jeff Hiller) who become dear friends. Audiences watch as they develop the sweetest bond that’s filled with lots of laughs and good vibes. “I hope that people come away with ‘never give up on yourself,’ because a lot of people do,” said Everett. St. Denis Medical | Peacock and Netflix Think of this as a hospital-centered version of The Office (another comfort TV favorite). This sitcom chronicles the day-to-day lives of nurses and surgeons as they navigate wacky medical scenarios and even wackier workplace dynamics. But we’d be remiss not to mention that there’s plenty of heart among the staff, who lean on each other as they care for patients. Stick | Apple TV A love letter to golf, Stick follows a former pro golfer seeking redemption by mentoring a teen prodigy who has his own complicated relationship with the game. The soun d track is stacked with hits, and you’ll never listen to “Cecilia” by Simon & Garfunkel the same way again. Survivor | Netflix (Select Seasons) and Paramount Plus (All Seasons) A show that just keeps on giving, Survivor has delivered over 50 seasons of real-life drama about “castaways” competing for a prize of $1 million. While the concept has remained mostly the same for more than two decades, every season delivers new personalities and social dynamics. Ted Lasso | Apple TV The epitome of comfort TV, Ted Lasso centers on an American football coach (Jason Sudeikis) who is hired to manage a British soccer team. Even if you’re not a sports fan, this four-season series is so charming and rich with wholesome humor that makes it a feel-good favorite for everyone. Tex Mex Motors | Netflix Watch old junkyard cars from Mexico get radically restored in Texas, thanks to a talented team of experts on Tex Mex Motors . While the car transformations are fun to watch (and very impressive), the restoration pros are the real stars of the show. The Dog House | HBO Max and Hulu ​If you haven’t watched The Dog House yet, you’re in for a treat. The unscripted show follows staff at a British animal rescue charity as they match pups with new pet parents. It’s a joy watching people light up when they fall in love with their new best friend — and of course, seeing the pups fall in love with their new best friends, too. The Durrells in Corfu | PBS and Prime Video The Durrells in Corfu is a British series based on memoirs about a family who left England for Greece in the 1930s. Not only is the story full of wit and heart, but it’s also set in the dreamiest of settings. And after you watch the show’s four seasons, we recommend checking out this documentary about the real Durrells . The Great British Baking Show | Netflix Of all the comfort shows streaming lately, The Great British Baking Show (titled The Great British Bake Off in the U.K.) takes the cake — pun intended. Each week, contestants bake all kinds of mouthwatering treats in hopes of making it to the finale, where one talented baker earns the coveted cake stand and is crowned winner. But unlike so many other competition shows that can feel cutthroat, the judges offer kind, constructive feedback, and the contestants often help one another finish their creations. You can stream most seasons on Netflix, including the most recent with new judge Nigella Lawson, a star addition as far as the Nice News team is concerned. Younger | Netflix In Younger , Liza, a 40-year-old mom (played by Sutton Foster), pretends to be in her 20s to land an entry-level assistant job at a publishing house in New York alongside Kelsey (played by Hilary Duff). A love triangle, book deals, and many stories of female friendship ensue over seven seasons of lighthearted TV. Highly recommend for fans of Lizzie McGuire .

Σε αντίθεση με τους συμβατικούς ηλεκτρονικούς νευρώνες, αυτές οι συμπεριφορές προκύπτουν φυσικά από τις μαγνητικές ιδιότητες της συσκευής, χωρίς να απαιτείται πολύπλοκο κύκλωμα ελέγχου…
items.descriptionOriginal: Researchers have designed an electronic neuron that combines two simple elements, a conventional transistor and a nanoscale magnetic device, to reproduce the behaviors of biological neurons. Unlike conventional electronic neurons, these behaviors emerge naturally from the magnetic properties of the device, without requiring complex control circuitry. The circuit can generate precisely timed electrical pulses that resemble those of biological neurons and, in a small demonstration, perform machine learning.

items.descriptionOriginal: Electrolyte additives designed to improve battery performance can instead shorten battery life when they are incompatible with each other. Researchers at the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST) have identified why protective layers inside batteries fail to form properly when certain additives are used together and have proposed a new additive to address this problem. The findings are expected to contribute to the development of electric vehicle (EV) batteries that retain their capacity over long-term use.

items.descriptionOriginal: Behind the electric grid upgrades driven by the artificial intelligence boom and the electrification of transportation lies an environmental concern: sulfur hexafluoride (SF₆), an extremely potent greenhouse gas. SF₆ is used in high-voltage electrical equipment for its insulating properties and in semiconductor manufacturing as an etching gas. It can trap about 24,300 times more heat than the same amount of CO₂ over 100 years.

items.title: Ένα Cocker Spaniel βιδώθηκε κατά τη διάρκεια μιας μετακόμισης το 2019. Επτά χρόνια αργότερα, ένα μικροτσίπ τον έφερε στο σπίτι.
items.titleOriginal: A Cocker Spaniel bolted during a move in 2019. Seven years later, a microchip brought him home.
items.description: Το 2019, μια οικογένεια στο Λος Άντζελες ετοιμαζόταν να μετακομίσει στο Σαν Ντιέγκο όταν το κόκερ σπάνιελ τους, το Corduroy, εξαφανίστηκε. «Η εξαφάνισή του ράγισε τις καρδιές τους, ειδικά τον καλύτερο φίλο του, τη μικρή κόρη της Samantha», έγραψε η Los Angeles Animal Services σε μια ανάρτηση στα μέσα κοινωνικής δικτύωσης. Μετακόμισαν χωρίς αυτόν και πέρασαν επτά χρόνια. Μετά, τον Οκτώβριο, ένα παλιό…
items.descriptionOriginal: In 2019, a family in Los Angeles was getting ready to move to San Diego when their cocker spaniel, Corduroy, went missing . “His disappearance broke their hearts, especially his best friend, Samantha’s young daughter,” Los Angeles Animal Services wrote in a social media post. They moved without him, and seven years passed. Then, in October, an older cocker spaniel came into LA Animal Services’ North Central Shelter . Nobody knows where Corduroy had been for all that time, but his microchip still led straight to his family, who were still living in San Diego. They drove up to get him. “They made the trip from San Diego to bring him home, and the reunion was filled with hugs, smiles, and happy tears,” the shelter wrote, according to KTLA . LA Animal Services shared two photos side by side: Samantha’s daughter as a little girl, hugging Corduroy on the steps, and the two of them together again seven years later. “Corduroy’s story is a powerful reminder: microchips help bring lost pets home, even years later!” the shelter added. It’s important to note that the chip only worked because the family’s contact information on it was still current. A microchip is just an ID number; if the phone number registered to it is no longer active, the scan leads nowhere. All six LA Animal Services shelters offer microchipping. View this post on Instagram The post A Cocker Spaniel bolted during a move in 2019. Seven years later, a microchip brought him home. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.title: Για γυναίκες Gen X με ηλικιωμένους γονείς, το σκίτσο «Sister» της SNL βρίσκεται πολύ κοντά στο σπίτι
items.titleOriginal: For Gen X women with aging parents, SNL’s ‘Sister’ skit hits way too close to home
items.description: Το Saturday Night Live κάνει περιστασιακά ένα κοινωνικό θέμα στο κεφάλι, τυλίγοντάς το με χιούμορ για να πει κάτι. Το σκετς «Sister» που προβλήθηκε στις 14 Νοεμβρίου 2026, μπορεί να είναι απλώς ένα από τα καλύτερα του. (Ή το χειρότερο, αν είστε μία από τις εκατομμύρια γυναίκες Gen X που βλέπουν τον εαυτό τους σε αυτό.) Το σκετς ξεκινά με έναν μεσήλικα που υποδύεται ο John Mulaney να ρωτά…
items.descriptionOriginal: Saturday Night Live occasionally hits a social issue right on the head, wrapping it in biting humor to make a point. The “Sister” skit that aired on November 14, 2026, might just be one of its best. (Or worst, if you’re one of the millions of Gen X women who see themselves in it.) The skit begins with a middle-aged man played by John Mulaney asking his elderly father if he’d taken his meds. When the dad says he doesn’t remember, Mulaney starts speaking to the camera in the style of a medical aid commercial: “My dad means the world to me. So when I noticed him start to slow down, I knew I needed to get him the best care possible. I didn’t want to put him in a nursing home, but a private health aide could cost thousands a week. I didn’t know where to turn. That’s when I heard about Sister. Sister is a live-in, 24/7 elder care provider that is completely free…and also your sister.” The ‘Sister’ skit says things that usually go unspoken The skit clearly states the expectations that so often exist as a subtext when daughters are automatically expected to take on aging parent caregiving duties: “Now I don’t have to worry about Dad getting the care and attention he needs, because my sister will do it, and I can get back to my life and the stuff I like to do.” “I love my mom more than anything. That doesn’t mean I want to help her in the bathroom. Sister doesn’t either, but she will, whereas I won’t.” “Simply text ‘Dad fell’ to Sister, and she will quit her job, break her lease, and move halfway across the country to take care of him. First, years of internalized sexism warps Sister’s brain into thinking caretaking is her responsibility and somehow not yours. Next, your text arrives, instantly activating her. And that’s it. You’re done for life. See you at the funeral.” “I used to get overwhelmed by my dad’s medications. Not Sister. She doesn’t get confused by that stuff at all. Or if she does, she hasn’t brought it up to me because I haven’t asked.” It’s just ouch after ouch, as brothers say out loud the things that usually go unspoken. In my friendship group, every one of us is doing, or did, the primary care of older parents with very little or no assistance at all from our brothers — ShazH @shazh.bsky.social (@ShazHaitch) November 16, 2026 The ‘daughter default’—why the ‘Sister’s SNL skit resonates The Sister “ad” is funny because it’s true. Most unpaid caregivers are women, and 62% of Americans agree there is an unspoken expectation that daughters will care for aging parents. Ironically, that truth also makes the skit not so funny. Comedy often holds up a mirror, and in this case, the Sisters who see themselves in it feel a tension between the “that’s so real” laughter of being seen and the frustration at the reality behind the portrayal. In other words, it hits too close to home. Sisters who serve as the default caregivers in their families weighed in: “As a Sister, this pissed me off almost as much as it made me laugh.” “As the caregiving sister, this triggered me SO BAD.” “This is SO real. I am oldest Sister. Which is basically the deluxe version.” “Not even satire, a much needed public service announcement on how bad this sucks to be me. Thank you to the writers.” “If a sketch was my life. I want to send this to my older siblings soooo bad.” from the makers of Sister , introducing: Eldest Sister — Jax (@jax_m6) November 16, 2026 Even those who aren’t Sisters themselves saw the reality in it: “Speaking as someone who inadvertently found himself in the role of ‘Sister’s Husband’ I can attest that this video is 100% accurate.” “Oh my god, this describes my mom helping with her mom from three states away when one brother lives barely 20 minutes away and one lives with my grandmother.” “As a younger brother to a sister, this made me deeply uncomfortable in the best way.” “As someone who works in a hospital as a nursing assistant, this is more reality than comedy.” In perusing hundreds and hundreds of comments, not one argued that the skit was inaccurate or unfair. How often does that happen? A love letter to default caregivers everywhere Right now, Gen X women are the ones most often in the Sister role, which feels a bit like a betrayal. Gen Xers grew up immersed in gender equality messaging, so finding this stage of life feeling so skewed on the gender front only adds to the feeling of unfairness when the work is uneven. Granted, a Sister’s siblings may not overtly think the things the brothers say in the skit, and the work being dumped in her lap may not be intentional. But the overwhelming response to the skit demonstrates that that’s very much how it feels. SNL writer Streeter Seidel, who co-wrote the skit with Mikey Day and Simon Rich, dedicated it to his sister Heidi. The fact that male writers came up with this uber-honest brilliance and boldly put it out there may offer some hope for Sisters everywhere. Written with @mikeyfuntime and the great Simon Rich (with an assist from Chase Rosenberg). Dedicated to my sister Heidi https://t.co/kn9f7ZVvKp — Streeter Seidell (@streetseidell) November 15, 2026 In some families, it may not be Sister, but Closest-in-Proximity Sibling who takes on the primary care duties for aging parents. Ideally, parental caregiving is a group effort among all siblings, and if one of them takes on extra due to ability or proximity, the others had better make darn sure they provide that sibling with some extra care and appreciation. Hopefully, this skit will help everyone with aging parents see that. The post For Gen X women with aging parents, SNL’s ‘Sister’ skit hits way too close to home appeared first on Upworthy .

items.title: Ο εκατομμυριούχος Kevin O'Leary προκάλεσε έναν Gen Zer που εργάζεται 80 ώρες την εβδομάδα. Η συζήτησή τους γυρίζει τα κεφάλια.
items.titleOriginal: Millionaire Kevin O’Leary challenged a Gen Zer who works 80 hours a week. Their debate is turning heads.
items.description: Στην εξαιρετικά δημοφιλή σειρά του YouTube Surrounded , ειδικοί ή γνωστές φιγούρες συζητούν γρήγορα με καθημερινούς ανθρώπους που βρίσκονται σε αντίθετες πλευρές ενός ζητήματος. Φιλελεύθεροι εναντίον συντηρητικών, πολιτικοί εναντίον μη ψηφοφόρων, επιχειρηματίες εναντίον αντικαπιταλιστών. Η ανατροπή; Οι ειδικοί υπερτερούν σε μεγάλο βαθμό, 20 προς ένα, εξ ου και το όνομα. Πρόσφατα, ο σταρ του Shark Tank, επένδυσε…
items.descriptionOriginal: In the wildly popular YouTube series Surrounded , experts or well-known figures debate rapid-fire with everyday people on opposite sides of an issue. Liberals vs. conservatives, politicians vs. non-voters, businessmen vs. anti-capitalists. The twist? The experts are massively outnumbered, 20 to one, hence the name. Recently, Shark Tank star, investor, media personality, and all-around multimillionaire Kevin O’Leary, aka Mr. Wonderful, stepped into the hot seat to take on 20 frustrated Gen Z workers . The results were absolute fireworks. Security guard working 80 hours a week challenges O’Leary’s wealth claims The format for Surrounded is as follows: The expert makes a claim in their area of expertise, and the twenty participants scramble to take them on in a head-to-head debate on that claim at the center of the stage. In one particularly fascinating moment of the episode, O’Leary claims that “Anyone in America can become wealthy if they work hard enough.” At one point, a young man sat across from him and introduced himself as Kieran. Like many in the crowd, Kieran took exception to Mr. Wonderful’s claim. “I’m gonna use myself as an example. I work 80 hours a week on average,” Kieran says, adding that he works as an unarmed security guard. Kieran says it’s impossible for him to simply work harder and get more done in less time, as it’s a timed patrol. With working 80 hours a week and spending more than half his income on rent, he has little time or money left to “work harder” and improve his situation. O’Leary challenges Kieran on his attitude, claiming he should push for a promotion, a manager role, or at least a raise. Kieran counters that he has, but there are only so many positions to go around. Meanwhile, he’s applied to hundreds of other jobs, looking for some upward movement, and can barely land an interview. O’Leary has made a whole career out of playing the heel. But in this surprisingly honest conversation, he seems to really try to help Kieran. “There’s somebody, somewhere that needs a manager of security guards, and you sound like you have the chops to do it,” he says. O’Leary advises going above and beyond: knocking on doors, making a self-promotional video. Kieran says there’s simply no job market anymore, and the opportunities O’Leary describes don’t exist. It’s an amazing back and forth that’s worth a watch. Kevin O’Leary gets CHALLENGED by a security guard who works 80 HOURS A WEEK after arguing that ANYONE can become WEALTHY through hard work, only for the guard to reveal that 55% of his income goes to RENT and he’s applied to HUNDREDS of jobs without success, questioning how much… pic.twitter.com/73NXCjlpEw — Killa (@KillaKreww) November 15, 2026 O’Leary isn’t wrong, he’s just a few decades too late O’Leary isn’t being the millionaire jerk in this exchange with Kieran, but he is showing his age. He’s spouting the typical Baby Boomer financial advice repeated by everyone from Dave Ramsey to Mark Cuban: work hard, skip the lattes, climb the ladder, and eventually become wealthy. What Kieran is exhausting himself trying to explain to O’Leary is that times have changed. One in 4 American workers say they have no opportunities for advancement in their current role. The odds are even longer for workers without a college degree or advanced education. That leaves many Gen Zers frantically job-hopping to find meager raises and better opportunities. But as Kieran explains, most applications are done online, where employers are overwhelmed with a staggering number of resumes. Many of the jobs Gen Zers like Kieran apply for aren’t even real, with so-called “ ghost jobs ” making the experience all the more frustrating. Meanwhile, wages have stagnated while the cost of living has soared. At 80 hours per week, a guy like Kieran simply doesn’t have time to knock on doors and network for a higher salary. He needs each and every one of those hours to afford groceries and a place to live, like much of his generation. Over 60% of Gen Z is considered “ rent-burdened .” Viral exchange highlights a broken system Though O’Leary’s suggestions might be out of date, he makes a point: should Kieran just give up and accept that he’ll never be able to afford a better life or find a different job? Asking for a promotion or making a video resume isn’t likely to move the needle. But he’s trying to tell Kieran to find a way to think outside the box and make people notice him. “You’re articulate enough to be a supervisor; you’re sitting here debating with me, and you’re doing a good job,” O’Leary says. “You’re going to find a better job, and you’re going to myopically focus on that, and you’re going to spend a fair amount of time making sure that happens.” O’Leary consistently appears dumbfounded that there is no upward mobility for high-performance employees. https://t.co/WLrxOz2ZxO — Joe Wargo (@JoeWargo22) November 15, 2026 The obvious takeaway is that Gen Zers like Kieran, and like the other people featured in the video, shouldn’t have to jump through absurd hoops to achieve a life they can afford. In O’Leary’s time, that meant burning the midnight oil and knocking on a few doors. In Kieran’s time, it means finding a way to separate from the pack of millions and millions of frustrated job-seekers. O’Leary’s message was surprisingly earnest, for him. But it would be an understatement to say that, since he built his own personal wealth decades ago, things have gotten much harder. items.descriptionOriginal: Somewhere right now, a home cook is crying over a cutting board. The onion always wins. Then comes the garlic, the oil, and a pan that needs babysitting. Italian cookbook author Marcella Hazan ‘s famous tomato sauce recipe skips almost all of that. You cut one onion in half, drop both pieces into a pot of tomatoes and butter, and walk away. About 45 minutes later, you fish the onion out. Hazan, who is credited with teaching Americans that great Italian food didn’t have to be fussy, published the recipe decades ago. And that onion, the one that doesn’t stick around for dinner, is the whole reason it works. When Hazan was newly married and about to leave Italy for New York, she asked her mother for the tomato sauce recipe she’d always loved. The answer was the usual Emilia-Romagna method: Sauté a chopped onion in butter until it turns deep gold, then add the tomatoes and cook them down. It was delicious, but Hazan soon found a more direct route. “Why chop and sauté the onion?” she thought. “I’ll just peel it and put it in the pot with the butter and tomatoes.” That single change produced the version that traveled the world, her husband Victor Hazan later wrote . What the onion is actually doing in there Think of the onion less as an ingredient and more as a seasoning. It goes into the pot the way a bay leaf goes into soup, gives up its flavor, and comes out before anyone grabs a bowl. Left in two big halves, the onion releases that flavor slowly. Over a long, gentle simmer, its sharp raw bite mellows into a soft sweetness that backs up the tomatoes without stealing the show . And that’s exactly why the low heat matters. “If we reduce too fast, then it doesn’t give the onion time to do its thing,” English chef April Bloomfield said while making the sauce for the PBS series American Masters . Why it leaves before dinner Pulling the onion keeps the spotlight on the tomatoes. No stray onion bits, and the tomato flavor stays bright. Of course, some cooks treat “remove the onion” as more of a suggestion. Why waste all that flavor when you could blitz it right back in? Well, one Food52 reviewer tried exactly that with one of the leftover onion halves and watched the bright tomato flavor slip away. “Essentially, it had turned it into a different sauce,” the reviewer wrote . Turns out Hazan knew what she was doing after all. Out of the pot doesn’t have to mean in the trash, though. Hazan’s recipe says to discard the onion, but plenty of cooks can’t toss something that soft, buttery, and tomato-soaked. “Then Hazan has you discard the onion, but I think you should actually eat it,” Food52 editor Kristen Miglore wrote in her Genius Recipes column in 2011. She suggested chopping it into a relish for grilled Italian sausage. Other home cooks smear it on crusty bread or stir it into a pot of chili . Marcella Hazan’s tomato sauce with onion and butter Four ingredients. That’s it. The pasta and a snowfall of grated Parmigiano-Reggiano are just for serving. Adapted from the version published by PBS . Ingredients 2 pounds fresh, ripe tomatoes or 2 cups canned Italian plum tomatoes with their juice 5 tablespoons butter 1 medium onion, peeled and cut in half Salt Directions Put the tomatoes, butter, onion halves, and salt in a saucepan. Cook uncovered at a very slow, steady simmer for about 45 minutes until “the fat floats free from the tomato,” as Hazan wrote. Stir now and then, mashing any big tomato pieces with a wooden spoon. Taste for salt and remove the onion. Toss the sauce with 1 to 1½ pounds of cooked pasta and serve with grated Parmigiano-Reggiano. Serves 6. It freezes well, too. Just be sure to pull the onion out before popping the sauce in the freezer. Yes, that’s a lot of butter Everybody doctors up tomato sauce. A splash of cream, a pinch of sugar, a Parmesan rind tossed in to simmer. But more than half a stick of butter and not a drop of olive oil? To plenty of cooks, that reads like a typo. And when the recipe caught on, some Italian Americans called the butter un-Italian . But Hazan didn’t see it that way. She came from Emilia-Romagna, a region of northern Italy where cooks reach for butter . Believe it or not, this is the toned-down version. Her first cookbook called for 1/2 cup of butter, a full stick. By the time the sauce landed in her 1992 book Essentials of Classic Italian Cooking , she’d cut it to 5 tablespoons. And the butter softens the tomatoes’ acidity , leaving the sauce richer and more rounded than any four-ingredient recipe has a right to be. The sauce for nights you’re running on empty You know those nights. The fridge is bare, you’re running on fumes, and DoorDash is calling your name. This sauce needs one pot, a few pantry staples, and 45 minutes of mostly ignoring it. No wonder it has stuck around. It’s the most popular tomato sauce in Food52’s archive , with nearly 600 reviews. Not bad for a vegetable that gets one cut, does all the work, and then gets kicked out of the pot. Whether it ends up on a slice of bread, in a relish, or in the compost bin, that onion has already earned its place at the table. The post An Italian cooking legend’s tomato sauce uses 4 ingredients. The onion comes out at the end. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: People love making connections . Friends, co-workers, and neighbors form the rich tapestry of our daily lives. Sometimes, you look at the Venn diagram of your social circle and realize: these two friends of mine are so alike , they just have to meet! You can already picture them hitting it off over shared hobbies, inside jokes, or ambitious professional goals. Introducing two people can be tricky. Photo credit: William Fortunato/pexels.com So you decide to play social matchmaker and introduce them at a party, lunch, or work event. “How can two people so similar not get along?” you think. Yet, according to communication specialists , well-meaning hosts often make one common mistake that can instantly spoil the entire interaction. The trap of putting your expectations upfront When we introduce two people we admire, we naturally want them to get along famously. In our excitement to bridge the gap, we often lay on the praise way too thick. We enthusiastically blurt out phrases like, “You two are bound to be best friends!” or “You are going to love each other so much!” It feels warm, polite, and encouraging in the moment. We tell ourselves that we’re giving them a head start. But etiquette experts warn that this well-meaning approach frequently backfires. According to etiquette expert Nick Leighton , putting lofty expectations upfront places immediate, awkward pressure on both parties. Suddenly, they are not just casually meeting a new acquaintance. Instead, they feel like they are auditioning for a predetermined role you already wrote for them. Both people become hyper-aware of trying to live up to your grand prediction. That sudden self-consciousness makes natural banter much harder to achieve. If the initial conversation hits a brief, quiet lull, an unspoken sense of disappointment may set in. They might even feel guilty for not sparking an instant, lifelong bond. That forced social pressure can quietly kill interest before it ever gets a fair chance to grow. How to make introductions feel effortless and natural Instead of hyping up the certainty of a lifelong friendship or predicting future business partnerships, communication experts recommend a much simpler, grounded approach. Focus on emphasizing specific, genuine, shared traits or passions —things that naturally connect the pair in the present moment. Instead of declaring them future besties, highlight a concrete mutual interest or funny coincidence. You might say, “Sarah, this is Mark. He is also obsessed with local pottery and just adopted a senior rescue dog.” Or, in a professional setting, keep it crisp and relevant. You could say, “David, meet Elena. She leads marketing for a local nonprofit, and you two both grew up in Ohio.” This simple shift works wonders. It gives both parties an easy, organic launchpad for real conversation, with no weird strings attached. It allows them to explore their own dynamic and connect comfortably at their own pace. If they click, it feels like their own exciting discovery rather than your assigned homework. Good social matchmaking is simply about opening the door, not pushing people through it. Next time you think, “These two have so much in common, they’re going to end up taking cruises around the world together in retirement,” take a step back. It’s more important to share a quick common thread and let real chemistry take the wheel. The post Etiquette expert says to avoid a common way of introducing people that feels polite, but often backfires appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: Researchers at the University of Surrey have developed a framework that could help wearable devices generate electricity from everyday movements and vibrations, reducing their reliance on batteries. Developed with university spin-out Z-PULSE, the model predicts how much power triboelectric nanogenerators (TENGs) can produce from mechanical motion. These lightweight, flexible devices generate electricity when two charged surfaces come into contact and separate. The new framework combines mechanical and electrical behavior in a single model, helping engineers understand energy losses and optimize generators to produce more power from irregular vibrations. Vibrations into electricity The new modeling framework could help engineers design more efficient devices capable of generating electricity from everyday vibrations. The technology focuses on TENGs, lightweight and flexible devices that convert mechanical movement into electrical energy. The framework predicts how mechanical vibrations are converted into useful electrical power, potentially supporting future battery -assisted or battery-independent wearable electronics and autonomous sensors . TENGs generate electricity through a process called contact electrification. When two different materials come into contact, they develop opposing electrical charges. Separating the surfaces creates a potential difference that drives electrical charges through an external circuit, producing electricity. The process is similar to static electricity generated when a balloon is rubbed against a sweater. Unlike conventional electromagnetic generators, TENGs can harvest energy from relatively slow and irregular movements. This makes them attractive for applications involving human motion, structural vibrations, and other low-frequency mechanical energy sources. However, predicting their actual electrical output has remained difficult because conventional circuit models often overlook the mechanical behaviour of the devices. The team addressed this limitation by developing a lumped electromechanical equivalent-circuit (LEEC) framework. The model combines the mechanical and electrical components of a TENG into a single mathematical representation, allowing engineers to examine how energy moves through the complete system. It incorporates parameters such as the device’s mass, spring stiffness, and mechanical damping, alongside electrostatic forces, surface charge density, and the changing distance between the charged materials. It also accounts for the electrical load connected to the generator. By representing mechanical components as their electrical equivalents, the framework allows researchers to use established circuit-analysis techniques to study energy conversion. This helps identify how much mechanical energy is transferred into electrical output and how much is lost through damping and other processes. “ A self-powered system becomes much more interesting when its generated signal is not treated only as electricity. The waveform also contains information about the mechanical environment that produced it. This creates the possibility of future devices that can harvest energy from their surroundings while sensing those surroundings at the same time ,” said Sajib Roy, a postgraduate research student at the university, in a statement . TENGs sense roads An important aspect of the approach is its ability to account for mechanical resonance. This occurs when the frequency of an external vibration approaches a device’s natural frequency, amplifying its movement. The researchers found that matching the operating frequency to this resonance can substantially improve electrical output by increasing the speed and amplitude of movement between the charged surfaces. Experimental tests using TENG devices with different mechanical properties showed close agreement with the model’s predictions. The researchers also examined how changes in oscillating mass, spring stiffness and damping influence resonance and power generation. In experiments involving different surface charge densities, four borophene-modified TENG devices produced progressively higher electrical outputs. The best-performing sample achieved an estimated energy-conversion efficiency of approximately 14.2 percent. The model also predicted a maximum cycle-averaged theoretical efficiency of around 54 percent under the investigated conditions. The researchers demonstrated another potential application by mounting a TENG on a bicycle mudguard to monitor road conditions. Vibrations generated while traveling over smooth, rough, and gravel surfaces produced distinct electrical signals. A classification model used these signals to distinguish among the three road types with 96.7 percent accuracy. The findings demonstrate that TENGs could potentially serve as both energy harvesters and self-powered sensing devices. The framework provides engineers with a way to optimize their mechanical and electrical characteristics together, rather than treating them as separate design problems.

What started with homemade thekua, gujiya and namkeen for her daughter’s birthday grew into MomsMade, a homegrown snacks brand now reaching over 3 lakh households across India. From a small kitchen in Bengaluru, Veena built a business dispatching 1,200–1,500 orders every day and earning around ₹2.5 crore in monthly revenue. Today, her children are helping take the dream forward. From Gopalganj, Bihar, to homes across India, Veena is doing more than building a business, she is keeping generations of homemade food traditions alive. #MomsMade #WomenEntrepreneurs #BiharEntrepreneur #Thekua #BihariFood #IndianEntrepreneurs #WomenInBusiness #HomemadeSnacks #BusinessSuccessStory #SmallBusinessIndia #BiharPride #FoodBusiness #TheBetterIndia

items.descriptionOriginal: "Six months ago, on the other side of the road, my life was something I wanted to come out of. Now, I have crossed the road, and everything is going well." On a busy road in Bengaluru's Koramangala, Parthiban sometimes looks at the BDO (Binder Dijker Otte) office differently. Today, he walks through its doors as an Article Assistant, one step closer to becoming a chartered accountant. But before joining BDO in April 2026, he knew the building from across the road. On one side was the Zepto store where he packed orders and the PG where he lived. On the other was the brightly lit BDO office. During tea breaks, he would look at it and wonder if he could one day work there. "I have crossed the road," he says. "Whenever I feel work pressure now, I think about the past. I have dreamt a lot and struggled a lot to reach this. " The road to that office involved failed CA Intermediate attempts, financial uncertainty, a close friend's bereavement, exhausting shifts at a warehouse, bicycle deliveries across Bengaluru and studying whenever he could find a few minutes. But Parthiban kept going. The dream that survived two failures Parthiban grew up in Kanchipuram, Tamil Nadu, in a family where resources were limited but his ambitions were encouraged. His father is a Nadaswaram player who studied until Class 3, while his mother, K Mahalakshmi, is a homemaker who studied until Class 12. As the first-generation graduate in the family, Parthiban knew that becoming a professional would mean a lot to his parents. Parthiban's journey from a delivery executive in Bengaluru to a CA Finalist was shaped by persistence, hard work and a determination to keep studying. His CA journey began with a decision he made during the COVID-19 period. In Class 9, unsure about what he wanted to pursue, he spent three days researching careers on his phone, from medicine and engineering to commerce. Eventually, he chose CA. He took science in Classes 11 and 12 on his mother's advice so he could keep his options open. After Class 12, he moved to Chennai and joined coaching for CA Foundation. The first step went remarkably well. Parthiban cleared Foundation in his first attempt with 305 out of 400, earning a distinction. His preparation was simple but consistent: attend classes, revise every day and take weekly tests. When accounts felt unfamiliar among students from a commerce background, he turned to YouTube. For some concepts, he watched five or six different videos until the basics became clear. CA Intermediate, however, proved much harder. The syllabus was larger, and the routine that had worked for Foundation became difficult to maintain. He failed his first attempt. The result affected his confidence deeply. "I lost myself actually," he says. "I faced many inferiority complexes, and that affected my preparation." Three months later, he attempted the exam again. He failed again. For his mother, those results were painful to watch. "His first CA Intermediate failure affected him deeply. He was completely heartbroken and emotionally shattered after seeing the result," she says. "Each time he checked the results portal and saw an unsuccessful outcome, it affected him greatly." Yet he never wanted to quit. "He never wanted to quit CA because it was a course he had chosen for himself," Mahalakshmi says. "However, after every unsuccessful attempt, he felt guilty about asking us to support him for the next exam ." By September 2025, circumstances at home also forced Parthiban to make another difficult decision. After giving his third attempt on 15 September, he travelled alone to Bengaluru the next day. He had one plan: find work, support himself and continue studying. Studying between shifts and deliveries Parthiban initially wanted to work as a delivery executive but could not find an electric vehicle. After two days of searching across areas such as JP Nagar and Jayanagar, he found work through a vendor at a Zepto store in Koramangala. His shift was officially 5 pm to 2 am. During busy periods, it stretched to 3 or 4 am, and sometimes even until 7 am. As an order packer, he spent six to seven hours running around the store, collecting and packing orders. The warehouse had several temperature-controlled zones. The freezer room was around 0 C, while the ice zone, where ice creams were stored, could be as cold as minus 15 C to minus 20 C. Late-night ice cream orders meant he sometimes had to search the freezing room around midnight. "After only two minutes, our nails become red and then it feels like something senseless," he recalls. Between late-night warehouse shifts and bicycle deliveries, Parthiban found small pockets of time to prepare for his CA Intermediate examinations. Even meals had to fit around the work. His PG was nearby, so when he got a few minutes, he would rush back, eat and return. For the first 15 days, he managed to study during the day and work at night. Then came another blow. A close friend he had met during CA Foundation lost her mother. Parthiban wanted to be with her and her family, but Zepto's strict working hours made it difficult to take leave. After working through the Diwali peak period, he resigned. He took a five-day break and then started working as a Blinkit bicycle delivery partner. He rented a cycle for Rs 600 a month because he did not want to depend on his parents financially. The work was physically demanding. On weekends, when incentives were higher, he sometimes rode 90 to 100 km in a day, working from the morning and returning to deliveries in the evening until 11 pm, midnight or even 1 am. But he carried his CA preparation into those hours too. Because Blinkit sometimes gave him only two or three orders an hour, he could get 20-minute gaps between deliveries. He used those breaks to watch marathon CA lectures on YouTube. Then, on 3 November 2025, the September exam results arrived and Parthiban had cleared one group of CA Intermediate. He continued working, however, because there was another attempt ahead. Then came an incident that made him rethink how he was spending those remaining weeks. One Sunday, after riding for hours, he was given a five-kilometre transfer order by another delivery executive. Already exhausted, Parthiban asked customer support and the store to cancel or reassign it. Instead, he was told that refusing could result in his ID being blocked. He called the customer. The first time, the call was cut. The second time, it happened again. On the third call, Parthiban says he literally begged the customer to listen. The customer told him he had one minute to explain and began counting. "1, 2, 3, 4…" The call was cut again. Five minutes later, the customer cancelled the order himself. "I was helpless," Parthiban recalls. "I was very much disturbed that day." That experience, combined with the limited time before his next attempt, pushed him to make a choice: go home and give the exam his full attention. Back home, he changed how he studied Back home, Parthiban had more than 45 days to prepare. This time, he did not simply study harder. He studied differently. After two unsuccessful attempts and a third in which he cleared one group, he went back to his mistakes and identified what needed to change. He divided his preparation into blocks of around 15 to 20 days per subject. He also changed his exam strategy. After two unsuccessful attempts at CA Intermediate, Parthiban reworked his study strategy and continued working towards his dream. In the tax paper, for example, he decided to attempt the smaller questions and MCQs first before moving to the compulsory question. The goal was to manage his time better and reach the 150 marks he needed. "I pointed out all the mistakes I had made in that attempt," he says. "I made some small changes, and that really helped me." The success of clearing one group had also given him confidence. Through it all, his parents continued to support him. "We never blamed or criticised him because we knew it could affect him emotionally, " says Mahalakshmi. "We understood the difficulty of the course, encouraged him to stay positive and reassured him that setbacks are a part of the learning process." After clearing both groups of CA Intermediate, Parthiban joined BDO's Bengaluru office as an Article Assistant on 2 April 2026. His sisters, Anuja and Supraja, were another important source of emotional support. Parthiban says they were people he could talk to during his difficult phases when he found it hard to share everything with his parents. Then, on 8 March 2026, came the result he had been working towards. He cleared the second group of CA Intermediate. Parthiban was now a CA Finalist. Six months later, he was on the other side The happiness at home was immense. "We were extremely happy and proud when he cleared CA Intermediate," Mahalakshmi says. "It felt like all his hard work, sacrifices and perseverance had finally paid off." A week later, Parthiban interviewed at four firms. He was selected by three. Parthiban joined BDO's Bengaluru office in April 2026, the same workplace he had once looked at from across the road during his tea breaks. One of them was BDO. He joined the Bengaluru office as an Article Assistant on 2 April 2026. The full-circle moment was not lost on him. Six months earlier, he had been working across the road. Now, he was walking into the very office he had once looked at during his tea breaks. His colleague Dharshan KS, a Senior Article at BDO, says Parthiban's determination was evident from the beginning. "He never lets circumstances limit his ambitions," Dharshan says. "His work ethic, humility and commitment to continuous learning stood out from day one." What also stood out was his kindness. "He connects easily with people from all backgrounds, is approachable, and helps create a positive and comfortable environment within the team." For Parthiban, being treated with respect had taken on particular meaning during his months in delivery work. During his time as a delivery executive, Parthiban was often treated differently because of the job he was doing. He recalls being scolded by motorists and encountering customers who treated him with suspicion. he office he once hoped to work in became his workplace when Parthiban joined BDO as an Article Assistant. At Zepto too, he experienced people using harsh words with him. He does not believe people need to be treated differently because of their education, profession or position. "Respect should be given to everyone," he says. "It should not be selective. Every person deserves some respect." What he wants other CA aspirants to know Parthiban is still an Article Assistant, with his CA Final examinations ahead. But the young man who once struggled with repeated failure now looks at setbacks differently. He calls his journey a "survival journey", one that taught him lessons far beyond his textbooks. His message to CA aspirants facing failure is simple. "Failures are common in CA," he says. "Even though we know that, whenever we see that result on the screen, it really affects us." But failure also taught him how precious success can feel. He explains it through food: the same meal may seem ordinary to someone who eats three times a day, but to someone who has gone without food for a week, it becomes something precious. For Parthiban, the road across from the Zepto store to the BDO office represents six months of hard work, difficult choices and a dream that stayed alive. "Once you face failure, you can experience the taste of success fully," he says. For Parthiban, that taste came after years of studying, failing, working, cycling through Bengaluru and finding lessons in places he never expected. And when work becomes difficult at BDO, he remembers the Zepto store across the road and the tea breaks when he wondered if he might one day work in the very office where he now sits. All images courtesy of CA Parthiban

items.descriptionOriginal: In the last couple of decades, many companies have reduced the heft of plastic bottles , cardboard boxes, paper envelopes, and other packaging materials, a strategy known as lightweighting. At first glance, this seems like a win-win: less material means lower costs and a lighter burden on the environment. But the approach may also backfire, a new study suggests. Researchers found that people are more likely to throw lightweight packaging away, and less likely to recycle it, compared to more substantial packaging materials. “Even well-intended sustainability practices can have unexpected negative consequences,” the researchers write. First, the researchers set out to determine the scope of the problem. A small pilot study at a university campus event and a larger week-long audit of trash and recycling bins on campus showed that lighter-weight recyclable plastic beverage containers were more likely to end up in the trash compared to more substantial plastic cups and bottles. “Once low-density packaging gets into consumers’ hands, it produces more waste, as consumers are more likely to improperly trash low-density versus high-density recyclable packaging,” the researchers write. Investigating causal relationships, the researchers concocted a laboratory study in which participants were asked to assess the properties of a piece of paper—either flimsy newsprint or sturdy cardstock—which they were instructed to dispose of at the end of the experiment. As expected, participants rated the thinner paper as lower quality than the thicker paper and were more likely to throw it in the trash at the end of the experiment—although a statistical analysis
