items.descriptionOriginal: Imagine receiving your monthly bank statement, opening the PDF on your phone and trying to find out how much money is in your account. But no matter how many times you try, the information remains out of reach. For a person with visual impairments, this can be an everyday experience. While a screen reader can read aloud the text on a phone or computer, it cannot always make sense of a PDF. The figures, tables and other information can remain inaccessible, leaving people dependent on someone else to read something as personal as their bank statement. The same problem extends to school textbooks, government forms and even company reports. When 17-year-old Yash Bhatnagar learnt about this gap, he began wondering if technology could help fix it. A self-taught coder who had already built a couple of digital tools, he decided to take on a problem that many people had overlooked. Visionably helps organisations convert inaccessible PDFs into documents that screen readers can navigate. Today, he is developing an AI-powered solution that helps convert inaccessible PDFs into documents that people with visual impairments can navigate using screen readers. But his idea goes beyond making a few documents readable. He wants organisations to rethink how they create and share information in the first place. From classroom tools to accessible PDFs Yash's interest in building things began early. Introduced to programming by his parents, he took a basic coding course on Khan Academy and continued learning independently, particularly during the COVID-19 pandemic. His parents recall how he took to programming almost immediately. "Even as a very young kid, he was demonstrating a penchant for building new technology," they share. Yash developed Visionably after discovering how difficult it can be for visually impaired people to access everyday digital documents. Rather than treating coding as an experimental hobby, Yash wanted to create products that solved problems for actual users. His first major project was LitGrades, an AI-powered flashcard generation platform launched in early 2023. After piloting it at his school, the platform grew to reach around 720 students, including learners from Ukraine. He then developed Silenttype, a real-time transcription tool that converted classroom lectures into notes that students could save in their digital libraries. In October 2025, while pitching the idea at IIM Ahmedabad, he began exploring how the tool could also help deaf users by transcribing spoken conversations and lectures. However, a conversation with the team there introduced him to a different challenge. "They told me that while they thought it was a good tool, there were more blind people who needed technology for OCR and converting PDFs into an accessible format," Yash recalls. The suggestion stayed with him. He was introduced to a few sample documents and began experimenting with ways to make them accessible. As he explored the problem, he realised that the challenge went beyond converting text into speech. Most PDFs are created without the underlying structure that screen readers need to interpret their contents. A document may look perfectly readable to a sighted person, with headings, paragraphs, tables and images arranged on a page. But without proper accessibility tags, a screen reader may not understand the reading order, distinguish between sections or describe visual elements. For someone relying on assistive technology, the result can be a document that is difficult, if not impossible, to navigate. Yash began working on a solution , initially with guidance from people in the accessibility community. One was Rashi, who works with V-Shesh, an organisation that supports people with disabilities and promotes accessibility. "The fact that persons with vision impairment have to struggle in educational institutions because a document was not accessible is something I have seen closely," Rashi says. She recalls students having to request assistance just to have documents read aloud to them. That experience made the problem particularly meaningful to her. As conversations between Yash and accessibility professionals continued, the initial prototype gradually evolved into Visionably. What makes a PDF readable to a screen reader? Visionably works primarily with businesses and organisations rather than asking individual users to fix documents themselves. Yash's approach is simple: make information accessible at the source. "It would make sense to make a news article accessible for every reader, but the newspaper should make it accessible themselves," he explains. Organisations share their PDFs with Visionably, which processes them through its AI-powered remediation engine. In simple terms, the tool helps add the information that screen readers need to understand how a document is organised. The technology identifies and adds details such as accessibility tags, reading order and descriptions for images. These changes help documents meet internationally recognised accessibility standards, including the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2 and PDF/UA, which outline requirements for accessible PDF documents. Once processed, the accessible files are sent back to the organisation. Yash says the turnaround can be around 48 hours, depending on the engagement. Building this technology, however, was not as straightforward as developing a tool that could extract text from a PDF. The AI-powered tool adds accessibility tags, reading order and image descriptions to PDF documents. Documents come in countless formats, with different layouts, tables, images and formatting styles. A system that works for a simple text document may struggle with a complex financial statement or a textbook containing several visual elements. "Because the number of PDFs on the internet is so large and the formats are so vast, it's very hard to account for every possible use case," Yash says. He worked through more than 1,000 test cases and iterations, regularly sharing documents with accessibility professionals and visually impaired users for feedback. He also received technical guidance from SaralX AI, a company working in the same space. According to Yash, the engine now succeeds on around 95% of the PDFs it is tested on. Crucially, the development process involves people who actually use screen readers. Yash says he has worked with a recurring visually impaired tester who reviews the documents and helps identify gaps that he might otherwise miss. Rashi recalls one instance when a visually impaired person tested an early prototype and pointed out several areas that needed improvement. "Yash said he wanted to meet again after a week. He sat through the night and by morning he had fixed everything," she says. For her, that willingness to act on feedback is what sets his work apart. Making websites easier to navigate for everyone Document remediation is only one part of Visionably's work. The venture also conducts automated accessibility audits of websites. These audits help organisations identify issues such as images without alternative text, missing accessibility features and elements that do not meet WCAG requirements. The system uses open-source technology alongside AI-based adjustments to examine websites and generate reports highlighting areas that need attention. For instance, simply checking whether an image has alternative text is not enough. The description itself must communicate what the image contains. An image labelled only as 'image' may technically have text attached to it, but it does little to help someone using a screen reader understand its purpose. Visionably's AI layer helps assess whether such descriptions are meaningful. Yash's Digital Banking Accessibility Index 2026 identified 2,221 accessibility barriers across 30 major Indian bank websites. Yash also released Outloud, a free, open-source tool that allows people to test whether their PDFs meet accessibility requirements. Unlike some existing tools that are limited to particular operating systems or workflows, Outloud works across Windows, Mac and Linux. Users can run accessibility checks, examine the results and even incorporate the tool into their own development processes. The idea is to make accessibility testing more widely available, including to developers and organisations that may not have the resources for expensive assessments. From children's books to banking websites One of Visionably's first paying clients is V-Shesh, which works with organisations on disability inclusion and accessibility. Through this engagement, Visionably has begun remediating documents on a per-page basis. The venture is also working with Pratham Books to make 10 children's books on its StoryWeaver platform accessible, pro bono. Six books had been completed at the time of the interview, with the remaining four nearing completion. For Yash, making these books accessible is particularly important because their stories should be available to children with visual impairments too. Rather than creating separate versions that readers have to search for, the plan is to make the accessible versions available directly on StoryWeaver. Alongside this work, Yash has been examining how accessible some of India's major banking websites are. His banking accessibility audit is another attempt to bring attention to gaps that often go unnoticed. The Digital Banking Accessibility Index 2026 assessed 30 major Indian bank websites, identifying 2,221 accessibility barriers. Yash selected banks based on factors such as their popularity, size and publicly available website traffic data. The automated audit examined multiple accessibility criteria, including whether images had appropriate alternative text and whether website elements met established standards. Through a collaboration with Pratham Books, Visionably is making children's stories accessible to young readers with visual impairments. The findings were shared with the respective banks, along with reports outlining the issues that needed attention. Yash says Kotak Mahindra Bank and Punjab National Bank responded, indicating that the concerns had been forwarded to the relevant teams. He plans to reassess the websites in December 2026 and publish a comparative report to track whether improvements have been made. For Rashi, this kind of accountability is important because accessibility cannot remain an afterthought. "I have interacted with so many children who volunteer with organisations working with persons with disabilities, but Yash is someone who is doing it genuinely, because he truly believes in it and not because it looks good on an application," she says. His next goal: Make accessibility part of the design Running a technology venture while studying in Class 12 is not without its demands. Yash spends around two hours on weekdays managing emails, reaching out to organisations, developing the product and planning new projects. Weekends are often reserved for longer work sessions and meetings. His parents, who are the company's directors because he is a minor, support him with business discussions and outreach. However, they say he makes the decisions for the startup, seeking their advice when needed. Yash hopes to make accessibility an integral part of how organisations design and share digital information, rather than an afterthought. Yash, meanwhile, sees plenty of room to expand. Over the next two years, he hopes to remediate at least 5,000 files and conduct 200 to 300 website accessibility audits. He is also exploring an assessment of shareholder and investor reports published by India's top 100 listed companies. His larger ambition, however, goes beyond fixing documents after they have been created. One conversation with a visually impaired professional who had previously worked in Microsoft Accessibility left a lasting impression on him. The person pointed out that accessibility is often treated as an afterthought rather than being built into the development process. That is a distinction Yash wants Visionably to address. "Our eventual goal is to become an accessibility design firm, where we don't look at accessibility as something that happens after files are created, but as part of the process when all of this actually begins," he says. All images courtesy of Yash Bhatnagar

items.descriptionOriginal: On 12 November, a pregnant woman lay on an operating table at the All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS) in New Delhi while surgeons performed something no Indian hospital had done before. Over six hours, they repaired a gap in her unborn baby's spine at 25 weeks of pregnancy , then closed the womb so that the pregnancy could continue. The institute announced on 14 November that this was India's first open foetal repair of a lumbosacral myelomeningocele, the most severe form of spina bifida. Professor Deepak Gupta, who led the neurosurgical component and is president of the Indian Society for Pediatric Neurosurgery, says, "It establishes an important new capability for foetal care and paediatric neurosurgery in India." Why doctors operate before birth In myelomeningocele, part of the spinal cord and its protective coverings pushes out through an opening in the spine. Doctors usually close it after the baby is born, but the institute said that exposure to amniotic fluid during pregnancy can cause progressive neurological injury. Surgeons used microsurgical techniques and ultrasound guidance to repair an unborn baby's spinal defect inside the womb. Photograph: ( TNIE ) "Affected children can develop paralysis or hydrocephalus, a build-up of fluid in the brain," the team says. In open foetal surgery , the surgeons open the mother's uterus to reach the defect, then carefully repair and cover the exposed spinal tissue in layers using microsurgical techniques before closing the uterus and abdomen, which lets the pregnancy continue under close supervision. Five weeks of rehearsal for one operation The operation followed more than five weeks of preparation that included detailed foetal imaging, counselling of the parents, anaesthetic planning and surgical simulations. "More than 30 doctors, specialists and nurses then took part, drawn from obstetrics, maternal-foetal medicine, neurosurgery, anaesthesia, plastic surgery, radiodiagnosis and neonatology, working with high-end microscopy and continuous ultrasound guidance at the Neurosciences Centre," the team says. More than five weeks of preparation and surgical simulations preceded the six-hour operation at AIIMS Delhi. Photograph: ( Newsonair ) AIIMS Director Professor Nikhil Tandon says the operation's complexity made teamwork decisive. "It is a matter of both pleasure and huge pride that such a complicated surgery could be done in this institution," he says. "It is a testimony to multiple very highly skilled people. Individually skilled and skilled as a team who could come together, sit, plan, collaborate, coordinate, and implement." He adds that the surgery is difficult even on a small child , and here the baby was operated on inside the womb. "Imagine the size. It is such delicate surgery," he says. "At least 36-37 doctors" were in the operating theatre, he says, including obstetricians, anaesthetists, radiologists, geneticists, neurosurgeons and plastic surgeons, along with the nursing staff and other OT staff. "It is very hard work, and it needed a lot of coordination. I think that teamwork was extremely important for us." Professor Neena Malhotra and Professor K Aparna Sharma headed the maternal-foetal medicine and obstetric teams. Sharma says the decision to intervene came from a careful assessment of the benefits and risks to both mother and baby, adding that safety depends on "detailed counselling, high-quality anaesthesia, and coordinated surveillance" before and after surgery. Professors Vimi Rewari and Mihir Pandia, with Drs Rashmi Ramachandran and Gyanendra Pal Singh, handled anaesthesia; Dr Shashank Chauhan led plastic surgery, and Drs Ramesh Agarwal and Deepika Kainth supported neonatology. Dr Anubhuti Rana, Dr Deepali Garg and Dr Saloni Kamboj helped screen and counsel the patient. From an idea in 2012 to an operating table Prenatal repair of myelomeningocele in humans was first performed in 1997, and more than 200 foetuses had undergone it before the trial began in 2003, so AIIMS joins a technique refined over nearly three decades. The evidence comes from the Management of Myelomeningocele Study, a randomised trial of 183 women published in 2011. By 12 months, 40% of children who had prenatal surgery needed a shunt to drain brain fluid, against 82% after postnatal repair, though the trial also recorded more preterm deliveries and uterine scar complications. Gupta recalled where it began. "Fourteen years ago, we spoke of the possibility of foetal spinal surgery at AIIMS," he said, and the institute now says it has the integrated expertise to assess and offer the repair to appropriately selected families. What the surgery cannot promise The doctors were careful not to oversell the spina bifida repair. Gupta described prenatal repair as a way to limit ongoing injury to exposed nerve tissue and to reduce the later need for a shunt, yet he stressed that it is not a cure and that long-term care from several specialities remains essential. The risks include premature delivery and complications from the uterine scar, which can affect later pregnancies, so the institute recommends it only for carefully selected pregnancies at specialised centres. The mother and baby remain under close observation until birth and through the newborn period, so the outcome of the repair is not yet known. The institute's statement does not name the family, but it confirms that the procedure was provided free of cost under the Janani Shishu Suraksha Karyakram, the government scheme offering free care to pregnant women and sick newborns who use public health facilities. Tandon says this was central. "We are immensely grateful that in this hospital, which is a publicly funded hospital, this entire work was done supported through a government scheme, at no cost to the patient," he says. "That, I think, is another very important point which needs to be communicated." Prevention matters as much, the team added. The neural tube closes about 28 days after conception, often before a woman knows she is pregnant, so doctors urged folic acid counselling before conception, food fortification with folates and stronger national surveillance of neural tube defects. The team's next goal, in its own words, is to make the surgery "safe and accessible" to the Indian families who may benefit from it. items.descriptionOriginal: A revolutionary new wearable patch could help people get more restorative sleep without medication or surgery. Developed by University of Texas researchers, the device uses gentle ultrasound to stimulate deep brain regions, helping participants enter REM sleep 43 minutes faster and remain there 16 minutes longer on average. The technology also showed promising effects on stress regulation and brain circuits involved in emotion.

items.descriptionOriginal: For Bhupen Rabha, a village elder in Assam, eating spiders is a food tradition he grew up with. He remembers how his parents and grandparents collected large, hairy spiders from the nearby forests, brought them home and prepared them as a seasonal delicacy. The spider, locally known as Bhaluk Makara , is the Indian Black Earth Tiger Spider ( Lyrognathus crotalus ), a species of tarantula native to Northeast India. Every year, between April and June, members of the Indigenous Rabha community in Assam's Kamrup (Rural) district collect these spiders from underground burrows along the edges of sal forests. Back home, they wash the spiders, soak them in hot water and fry them in mustard oil with salt and garlic powder. The dish is traditionally enjoyed with locally prepared rice beer. But why do they eat spiders? For the Rabha families who follow this practice, the answer lies in generations of food knowledge, the seasonal availability of the spiders and their close relationship with the surrounding forests. In August 2026, a study published in the Proceedings of the Zoological Society documented the community's consumption of this particular spider species for the first time in scientific literature. The research offers a closer look at how this food tradition has survived across generations, while raising important questions about the conservation of the species. How are these forest spiders collected and cooked? Around 65 kilometres southeast of Guwahati lies Mouman village, where members of the Rabha community live close to forests dominated by sal trees. Here, Bhaluk Makara lives in underground burrows. Its local name comes from its appearance. Bhaluk means bear, referring to the spider's large, black body covered in dense hair, while Makara means spider. To understand the community's relationship with the species, researchers Jyotiprakash Boro, Kuldeep Bora, Chandramita Boro and Samir Terdalkar conducted fieldwork between April and June 2025. They interviewed 34 Rabha community members, including village elders and experienced collectors, to understand when the spiders are gathered, how they are prepared and how the practice has been passed down. According to the villagers, the spiders are particularly abundant during April and May, making these the preferred months for collection. Collectors typically venture into the forests for three or four days a month during the peak season. Depending on availability, a single outing can yield around 20 to 30 spiders. Finding them requires familiarity with the forest. Collectors identify burrows along the forest fringes and either carefully dig into the ground or insert a wooden stick to encourage the spider to emerge. Once collected, the spiders are brought home, washed and repeatedly soaked in hot water for several minutes. They are then fried in mustard oil for approximately seven to 10 minutes until browned, with salt and garlic powder added for flavour. For families who have followed this practice for generations, collecting Bhaluk Makara involves knowledge of the spider's habitat, seasonal availability and preparation methods learnt from their elders. Between April and June, members of the indigenous Rabha community venture into areas adjoining sal forests to collect a large, dark, hairy spider from its burrow. Photograph: (Jyotiprakash Bora; iStock) Why has the Rabha community been eating spiders for generations? For the Rabha community, Bhaluk Makara is part of a wider food culture closely connected to the surrounding forests. Agriculture is an important livelihood, while fishing, livestock rearing, weaving and gathering forest resources are also part of community life. Rice is a staple food, accompanied by fish, meat, vegetables and locally collected edible plants. Bhaluk Makara belongs to this tradition of preparing foods available in the local environment. The practice has been passed down through generations, with older family members teaching younger ones where to find the spiders and how to prepare them. Bhupen Rabha told Mongabay India that the tradition had been passed down orally within the community. "The spider was regularly collected and eaten by our parents and grandparents as a seasonal delicacy," he recalled. And the tradition continues among younger community members. Ashok Rabha, a spider collector in his early 20s, described gathering spiders as an enjoyable shared experience and "a kind of rite of passage". For him, searching for burrows, collecting the spiders and eating them together is also a way of participating in a practice learnt from earlier generations. Rohini Kumar Nongbag, another experienced collector, told Mongabay India that younger people continue to collect the spiders during the pre-monsoon months. These accounts show that the practice remains part of community life, rather than something remembered only by older generations. However, researchers point out that the tradition may be limited to particular Rabha villages and households, rather than being followed by the entire community. Similar food practices have also been documented elsewhere in Northeast India. In March 2026, a study published in Frontiers in Sustainable Food Systems recorded the consumption of two species of orb-weaver spiders among Indigenous communities in Nagaland. Known locally as siyanky in the Lotha Naga language, these spiders are prepared using ingredients such as ginger, chillies and bamboo shoots. Researchers interviewed 33 people and found that knowledge of collecting and cooking the spiders was similarly passed down through generations. Although the species and recipes differ, both studies show how traditional food practices are connected to local biodiversity and the knowledge communities have developed over time. Its local name, Bhaluk Makara, refers to its bear-like appearance, with its relatively large, black body covered in dense hair. Photograph: (EastMojo) Can this food tradition continue while protecting the spiders? While the August 2026 study has documented an established food tradition, it has also highlighted how much remains unknown about the species. Within the Rabha community, Bhaluk Makara is regarded as a nutritious seasonal food. However, its nutritional composition has yet to be established through laboratory testing. The researchers also found no reported medicinal use of the spider among the community members interviewed. Another important question concerns the spider's population. Some collectors believe the species remains as abundant as it was years ago. Manoj Rabha, who has been collecting spiders for around 12 years, told Mongabay India that he has observed no noticeable decline. According to him, experienced collectors can still gather as many as 30 spiders during an outing. But these observations have yet to be supported by scientific population surveys. Jyotiprakash Boro, a wildlife biologist and research scholar at Fergusson College, Pune, explained to Mongabay India that the researchers had not independently assessed the spider's population or abundance. Scientists still need to understand how many spiders inhabit these forests, how quickly they reproduce and whether repeated collection affects their numbers. This is particularly relevant because some tarantula species grow slowly and take years to reach maturity, potentially making them vulnerable to excessive collection. Importantly, the study does not establish that the Rabha community's existing harvesting practices are harming the spider population. Instead, the researchers have called for further studies into the species' ecology, population dynamics, nutritional composition and conservation status before drawing conclusions about sustainability. For Bhupen and other members of the Rabha community, Bhaluk Makara remains a familiar seasonal food, connected to the forests around their villages and the knowledge they have inherited. The new research brings that knowledge into the scientific record, while opening up opportunities to better understand the spider and its habitat. It also highlights the importance of documenting Indigenous food traditions through the experiences of the people who practise them, so that both their cultural knowledge and the biodiversity connected to it can be better understood and protected. Sources: 'First Record on the Traditional Consumption of the Indian Black Earth Tiger Spider (Lyrognathus crotalus Pocock, 1895) Among the Rabha Tribe from Northeast India' : By Jyotiprakash Boro, Kuldeep Bora, Chandramita Boro and Samir Terdalkar, Published on 18 August 2026 'Edible spiders: an unconventional source of nutrition and therapeutic agents' : By Lobeno Mozhui, Kekhesino Sale, L. N. Kakati, Published on 9 March 2026 'For the Rabhas of Assam, this giant spider is a seasonal delicacy' : By Roopak Goswami, Published on 24 August 2026

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Mushroom Coffins and Green Burial Give Families a Soil-Enriching Choice Reading Time: 3 minutes Mushroom coffins and green burial options let families return nutrients to the soil. Mushroom coffins and green burial options give families a new way to care for the planet. Loop Biotech , a company in Delft, the Netherlands, grows these products from living mushroom roots. The company says traditional funerals can harm the environment. It points to cutting old trees, releasing carbon dioxide, and adding toxic chemicals to soil. Loop Biotech wants to offer a gentler choice. Interest in greener funerals is growing. A 2023 report from the National Funeral Directors Association found that 60% of consumers would explore green funeral options. That is about six in every ten people, so mushroom coffins and green burials meet a real demand. The idea began at Delft University of Technology. Founders Bob and Lonneke Hendrikx were graduating there when they asked a simple question: Could a final act help the earth instead of harming it? They found an answer in mycelium, the root network of mushrooms. It grows underground and breaks down dead plant matter. As it does, it releases nutrients that feed new life. Mycelium is known as one of nature’s biggest recyclers. Researchers have only recently given it close attention. For years, many of them focused on plants and animals above ground. Loop Biotech grows its products from local mushrooms and upcycled hemp fibers. Upcycled means the fibers are reused instead of thrown away. Hemp is a tough plant often used for rope and cloth. The growing process takes just seven days. Trees used for traditional coffins can take many decades to grow. That difference shows how quickly this material can be made. Once the coffin is buried, it begins to break down. The company says it biodegrades in about 45 days. Mushroom coffins and green burial materials like these return to the soil faster than most wood and metal. The coffin is also strong. Hendrikx says it can carry about 440 pounds (200 kilograms). He adds that people are often surprised by how soft and sturdy it feels. The company invented the world’s first mushroom coffin, called the Loop Living Cocoon. It also makes the Loop EarthRise and the Loop ForestBed. The company describes its products as patented and award-winning. Mushroom coffins and green burial options now include the Loop EarthRise, the world’s first urn made from mushrooms, grown in seven days from local mushrooms and upcycled hemp fibers to nourish the earth and grow a tree in your memory. Photo courtesy of Loop Biotech . Each product is 100% natural and biodegradable. Biodegradable means it breaks down naturally over time. The company also says its products enrich the soil. Soil-enriching is a bold claim, so families should look at the details. Asking a funeral provider about materials, local rules, and cemetery policies is a smart first step. Green burial is a broader movement. It generally avoids embalming chemicals and uses naturally biodegradable materials. Mushroom coffins and green burial fit together because both aim to leave the ground healthier. Why does this matter to families? Many people want a funeral that matches how they lived. For someone who loved gardens or forests, a soil-enriching option may feel personal. Loop Biotech describes its approach as working with nature rather than against it. The founders chose living organisms over dead materials. That idea shapes every product the company grows. The founders describe their mission as turning endings into new beginnings. This view invites people to think about death differently. It treats a funeral as part of a natural cycle. The company grows its products at a facility in Delft, close to where the founders studied. Local mushrooms keep the process tied to the region. That choice also supports the company’s goal of a positive footprint. A footprint is the mark people leave on the environment. The company wants that mark to be positive. It aims to return nutrients to the soil. Demand is spreading beyond Europe. Hendrikx estimates it has sold more than 2,000 coffins in Europe and has started selling in North America. Mushroom coffins and green burial alternatives are now reaching families on both continents. The company shares a brand video. It tells the story behind the products and the people who make them. For more detail, people can watch a TEDx talk by Bob Hendrikx. TEDx is an independently organized event that follows the TED talk format. He explains how mycelium works, how the products grow in seven days, and his vision of a regenerative world that restores natural systems. Mushroom coffins are one of several ideas for gentler goodbyes. Families are also finding new ways to honor loved ones while protecting the planet. Choosing a funeral involves many feelings and practical questions. Families who want an earth-friendly path now have more to consider. Mushroom coffins and green burial may help more people leave a positive mark. The post Mushroom Coffins and Green Burial Give Families a Soil-Enriching Choice appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: You changed your routine. You started eating better. You started moving more. At first, the weight came down. Now? Nothing. So what are you doing wrong? Maybe nothing. A plateau doesn’t mean you’ve stopped doing the right things. As weight changes, energy needs, sleep, stress, everyday movement and sustainability may all affect progress. Weightchange isn’t always a straight line. So is the answer to eating less and exercising harder? More restrictions may not address what is actually getting in the way. That’s when a doctor becomes useful, to review your weight history, what you’ve already tried, your health, your sleep and lifestyle, and what may be making progress harder to sustain. Keep your balanced meals, regular movement, strength activity and consistent sleep in place. If your weight stays stuck despite sustained effort, ask a qualified doctor about possible barriers and long-term weight-management options. A plateau is information, not a verdict. And medical help is not cheating. Talk to a qualified doctor about your metabolic health. Apni metabolic health ke baare mein ek qualified doctor se baat kariye. This is general information, not a diagnosis or medical advice. #CountWhatMatters #WeightPlateau #WeightManagement #HealthJourney #metabolichealth [weight loss plateau, why is my weight not moving, weight stuck despite diet and exercise, plateau is not failure, weight management India]

items.descriptionOriginal: I t is a Tuesday morning at Against Da Grain, a barbershop on a quiet street on Staten Island’s North Shore. Owner Sean White is rounding off a cut for a middle-aged Black man while another customer waits nearby. Around them, hairstylists work through a stream of clients; conversations move between jokes, social issues and the ordinary problems — and pleasures — of life. “It’s always usually like a community conversation inside of a barbershop,” White says. The shop hosts back-to-school giveaways, free haircut events and Christmas toy distributions, and partners with local organizations to connect residents with resources. White describes the shop as “like a third party to the community.” Against Da Grain was one of 22 Staten Island barbershops that participated in a hypertension screening program. Credit: Tolu Olasoji That intermediary role also creates an opening for health care: a way to reach Black men through a place and relationships already woven into their everyday lives. Dr. Joseph Ravenell is the principal investigator of the Community-to-Clinic Linkage Implementation Program , or CLIP, which brought hypertension screenings into barbershops as part of an American Heart Association study. He remembers going with his father to Mr. Mike’s shop every other Saturday, where the same men returned over months and years. That repetition, he says, builds “a level of trust, a level of camaraderie” that can be difficult to reproduce in health care. Men talked there about sports, politics and relationships, but also about health, and Ravenell was struck by how comfortable they were discussing intimate concerns — and how closely they listened to their barber. “It’s been said to me many times that many Black men trust their barber more than they trust their doctor,” he says. Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] CLIP sought to build on that familiarity as a way to reach people with undiagnosed hypertension. The condition is both common and easy to miss. About six in 10 non-Hispanic Black men in the United States have hypertension, according to federal data. Yet high blood pressure often produces no symptoms. Among men ages 18 to 39 who have hypertension, the federal data found, fewer than one in four know they have it . Routine access to health care can make early detection more likely, but access is only part of the problem. A 2019 study linked medical mistrust and perceived racism in health care with delayed checkups and blood-pressure screening among Black men. “It’s always usually like a community conversation inside of a barbershop,” says Sean White. Credit: Tolu Olasoji Led by NYU Langone in partnership with Community Health Action of Staten Island (CHASI), CLIP brought blood-pressure screening and health support into 22 Black-owned barbershops from Staten Island zip codes with high hypertension prevalence . Against Da Grain was one of them. W hite’s appointments that Tuesday often stretched beyond 30 minutes. “The barber chair is perfectly set up for measuring blood pressure,” Ravenell says. Some patients experience what’s known as “white coat syndrome,” meaning the stress of a clinical setting causes their blood pressure to rise temporarily. By contrast, getting a haircut gives someone time to sit and grow comfortable before being screened, so with proper technique, a reading taken at the barber shop may better reflect their usual levels. The challenge, Ravenell adds, was to “leverage what’s special about the barbershop without ruining what’s special about the barbershop.” Unlike in a clinical setting, getting a haircut gives someone time to sit and grow comfortable before being screened. Credit: Tolu Olasoji During CLIP, local Black male community health workers measured patrons’ blood pressure, counseled them, and connected them with medical and social services. Barbers encouraged customers to participate, but screenings were offered without pressure. “I allowed the men to decide whether they wanted to engage with me,” says a community health worker. Importantly, the community health workers were often themselves customers at the participating barbershops and knew the barbers and customers. Ravenell says that familiarity meant “their presence is not an intrusion, as it might be for someone with a white coat.” Across the program, 636 men were screened. Four hundred sixty-one were found to have elevated blood pressure or untreated stage one hypertension, 430 of whom enrolled in the study. Participants were 38 years old on average; only 24 percent reported having a primary care provider, and about half had health insurance. The study followed up with enrolled men at six-month intervals through 18 months, even after recruitment at individual shops had ended. At 18 months, community health workers obtained a repeat blood-pressure reading from 96 percent of participants. That level of follow-up, Ravenell says, is unusual and difficult to achieve in a long-running study. Dr. Chidinma Ibe, a community health workers researcher at the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Equity, calls the figures “extremely, extremely impressive,” adding that they reinforce the value of meeting people where they are. D espite these successes, however, CLIP did not produce the primary result researchers had hoped for . At 12 months, participants’ systolic blood pressure had changed little. Fewer men met the study’s definition of incident stage two hypertension at 12 months, but the difference was no longer statistically significant at 18 months. Dr. Ibe says that given that the intervention was among men with elevated blood pressure or untreated stage one hypertension rather than severely uncontrolled disease, the limited movement in its main blood-pressure outcome was “not terribly surprising.” The challenge for CLIP, notes Dr. Joseph Ravenell, was to “leverage what’s special about the barbershop without ruining what’s special about the barbershop.” Credit: Tolu Olasoji For Derek Griffith, a University of Pennsylvania professor who studies Black men’s health, success in simply reaching men is separate from controlling their blood pressure. He says the major determinants of blood-pressure control remain in what men experience outside both barbershops and clinical care. Dr. Idris Robinson, research project manager for Penn’s Program for Research on Men’s Health, likewise cautions against treating the barbershop itself as the intervention. “The blood pressure outcomes weren’t rooted in some magical equation where barbers plus Black men equals guaranteed improvements in Black men’s health,” he says. Sustained engagement, he argues, also depends on collaboration among academic and community partners, barbers’ relationships with clients, and a wider support network. “That infrastructure is critical.” That becomes crucial after an elevated reading. When this occurred with CLIP participants, community health workers explained what the number could mean and encouraged medical follow-up. When it came to a referral, notes Joseph Ebron, CHASI’s director of health equity, “We would let them know what we offer, but it was up to them to take it.” Credit: Tolu Olasoji Even when people wanted help, navigating existing services could complicate the handoff. Workers sometimes met people who thought they lacked coverage, only to discover they were already enrolled elsewhere but were not getting the help they needed. And because they were already attached to another provider or organization, CHASI could not always simply move them into a different service. “We can’t just, like, snatch them,” says Ebron. Ibe points to a structural problem behind that handoff: the fragmented American health care system. Insurance issues, the absence of an established primary care relationship, and weak connections between community organizations and clinical teams can all interrupt the route to care. “If the [community health worker] isn’t employed by that clinic, there’s only so much they can do,” she says. Sustaining even the community side required labor. Active recruitment through Against Da Grain lasted about two months. “We did it for some time without receiving any type of payments,” says White, adding that the program brought “a lot of extra work.” CHASI adapted around the business in real-time: For instance, Ebron says to work around Against Da Grain’s preferences, they screened outside, where workers could pull up a small mobile health unit and barbers could direct interested customers to it. Workers learned to take up less space, getting rid of tables and flyers in favor of a simpler setup: a blood-pressure monitor and materials carried in a bag. Though CLIP is now over, there are larger screening events every two to three months and health workers can return to shops when requested. Credit: Tolu Olasoji Ravenell sees funding — and therefore sustainability — as the broader limitation. When CLIP ended in September 2025, he says Staten Island screening partners continued some services “essentially pro bono” during a funding gap. His team has since received two new NIH grants to build on CLIP’s infrastructure and train community health workers to screen in barbershops for diabetes and diabetic eye disease. For now, CLIP itself is over, though Ebron says CHASI conducts larger screening events every two to three months and can return to shops when requested. Whether the model can travel is another question. Ravenell says Staten Island had an advantage before CLIP began: CHASI had already spent more than 30 years working in the borough through community health workers. “Replicated, yes, easily, no,” Ebron says, because success depends on what already exists locally. CLIP reinforced White’s sense of responsibility to the community he has served for more than 35 years, while sharpening his awareness of the health concerns moving through it. “It helped me realize how many people have elevated levels,” he says. Join Cancel anytime Around noon at Against Da Grain, White’s final appointment brings in a young couple and their son, there for the boy’s first haircut. His mother livestreams the occasion to relatives. When the boy climbs down, his father takes his place in the chair. One generation giving way to another, if only for a haircut. items.title: Η άνετη εμφάνιση των καφέ επισκευής
items.titleOriginal: The Cozy Emergence of Repair Cafés
items.description: Στα υπόγεια των εκκλησιών και στις κοινοτικές αίθουσες, οι Αμερικανοί συγκεντρώνονται όχι μόνο για να επισκευάσουν σπασμένες λάμπες και ραγισμένες καρέκλες, αλλά για να απωθήσουν μια οικονομία που επωφελείται από τη μοναξιά και τη σπατάλη. Όταν η Lilly Pettus έφερε μια καρέκλα τραπεζαρίας -- μετακόμισε σε έξι πολιτείες για τριάντα χρόνια, κρατώντας στο ξύλο της το βάρος του οικογενειακού γέλιου και της σκληρής συνέλευσης…
items.descriptionOriginal: Across church basements and community halls, Americans are gathering not just to fix broken lamps and cracked chairs, but to push back against an economy that profits from loneliness and waste. When Lilly Pettus brought a dining room chair -- moved across six states over thirty years, holding in its wood the weight of family laughter and hard conversations -- to a repair caf in Decatur, Georgia, she left with something more than a mended joint: strangers' hands had pressed her family's history back together. "When a product breaks and you have to throw it away, it's very lonely," says Martine Postma, who founded Repair Caf International in 2010, and the repair caf s she helped seed around the world are a quiet argument against that loneliness. In neighborhoods where the need is economic as much as environmental, and in ones where it is sentimental, the impulse turns out to be the same: a refusal to let things, and the connections they carry, be so easily discarded. What these gatherings reveal, almost incidentally, is that the skills of care have never really disappeared; they've just been waiting for a place to gather.

items.description: Στα 48 της, μετά από 19 χρόνια στην τάξη, η Ruksana Begum βρέθηκε να προετοιμάζεται για μια διαφορετική εργάσιμη μέρα. Τον Νοέμβριο του 2019, ξεκίνησε το Ghar Batti Food Service με έναν μέτριο στόχο: να μετατρέψει το φαγητό που της άρεσε να φτιάχνει σε βιοπορισμό. Οι πρώτοι πελάτες αγόραζαν γνωστά γεύματα, όχι μια μεγάλη νέα ιδέα. Η Begum, τώρα 55 ετών, είχε περάσει 19 χρόνια…
items.descriptionOriginal: At 48, after 19 years in the classroom, Ruksana Begum found herself preparing for a different kind of working day. In November 2019, she started Ghar Batti Food Service with a modest aim: to turn the food she loved making into a livelihood. The first customers were buying familiar meals, not a grand new concept. Begum, now 55, had spent 19 years teaching before resigning in 2019. Her children encouraged her to take her cooking beyond the family kitchen, repeatedly telling her that people would enjoy what she made. She was not certain the venture would work. A new beginning after 19 years of teaching Cooking was not an unfamiliar skill that she had to acquire for the business. Begum credits her mother-in-law with teaching her recipes and techniques that continue to shape her food. "My mother-in-law taught me a lot about cooking. I learned all these dishes and techniques from her, and I still carry those things with me in my cooking today," she told Startup Pedia. She chose the name Ghar Batti to keep that domestic connection visible. 'Ghar' means home, while 'Batti' is the Kashmiri word for rice. The name reflected what she wanted customers to receive. Cooking was not an unfamiliar skill that she had to acquire for the business. Begum credits her mother-in-law with teaching her recipes and techniques that continue to shape her food. Photograph: ( startuppedia ) The business began with little financial outlay. Begum bought a tiffin box and used the gas, spices, ingredients and kitchen equipment already available at home. She described the initial investment as almost zero, but was clear that the work itself demanded time and effort. She initially handled the work largely alone, with her husband's support; other family members joined as orders grew. The first model was a tiffin service. It brought in customers, but the routine of preparing and delivering meals every morning and evening was demanding. Individual orders ranged in value from less than ₹100 to ₹2,000, depending on what customers wanted. After running the service for about a year, Begum began looking for a way to make the work more flexible without giving up the business she had started. From a small tiffin service to catering for 200 people The shift came through customers who had already tasted her food. They began asking her to prepare meals for special occasions and larger gatherings. Instead of relying only on daily tiffin deliveries, Begum started accepting catering orders for events. Ghar Batti now caters to events and supplies food to hospitals, schools, banks and offices, according to Begum. She sometimes handles 10 to 12 events in a month, although the number varies. The business can cater for up to 200 people at a single even t, giving the home-based operation a reach far beyond its first tiffin customers. She chose the name Ghar Batti to keep that domestic connection visible. 'Ghar' means home, while 'Batti' is the Kashmiri word for rice. Photograph: ( NDTV ) The menu carries both familiar Indian preparations and dishes associated with Kashmir. Customers can order rogan josh, yakhni, dum olav and mirchi korma, alongside palak paneer, chicken 65, chilli chicken and butter chicken. In winter, the menu includes harissa, a traditional Kashmiri meat dish, as well as pickles, smoked fish and other local preparations. The challenges of building a business at 48 Despite the expansion, Begum says she wants the food to remain home-cooked. Ghar Batti takes advance bookings through phone calls, WhatsApp and social media, preparing quantities to match each order rather than operating as a dine-in restaurant. She also says the kitchen does not use preservatives or artificial colours. The venture has grown beyond a one-person operation , too. Begum now works with a team of four: three women who help prepare food for bulk orders and one delivery worker. She says the business also brings work to people in its supply chain, including butchers, fish vendors and vegetable sellers. Repeat customers and word-of-mouth referrals have brought in orders. Her next ambition is to grow without losing the way Ghar Batti works. Begum hopes to take on as many as 20 catering events a month while continuing to operate from home. She remains cautious about borrowing money and is assessing how much the business can expand with the resources she has. The tiffin box that helped her test the idea has given way to larger orders, a small team and institutional clients. Begum's advice to others considering a late start is simple: "There is no age limit." Sources: ' She Quit Teaching at 48 to Start a Tiffin Service, Today Her Srinagar-Based Small Business Handles 10–12 Events a Month ': by Tauseef Ahmad for Startup Pedia, published on 25 October 2026 ' At 48, This Kashmiri Teacher Started A Food Business From Home. Today, It Serves Hospitals And Banks ': by NDTV Food Desk for NDTV Food, published on 27 October 2026 ' Kashmiri Woman Left Teaching To Start Tiffin Service, Now She Is Catering 10-12 Events Every Month | The Ghar Batti Story ': by Swati Kumar for The Daily Jagran, published on 28 October 2026 ' Cloud Kitchen Entrepreneurship ': Centre for Career-Counselling, Coaching and Placement, University of Kashmir. items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Extended Producer Responsibility Laws Worldwide Now Cover More Than 70 Countries Reading Time: 3 minutes Extended Producer Responsibility laws worldwide have expanded from a single German packaging rule in 1991 into a global compliance landscape spanning more than 70 countries today. Extended Producer Responsibility laws worldwide shift the financial and physical burden of waste management from governments and taxpayers to the companies that manufacture and sell products. Under these laws, producers must collect, recycle, and properly dispose of the packaging and products they put on the market, fundamentally changing the economics of how goods are designed and sold. The concept traces back to Germany’s Packaging Ordinance of 1991, the world’s first EPR regulation. At the time, packaging waste accounted for roughly half of landfill volume and a third of total waste in Germany, pushing national landfill capacity toward its limits and forcing policymakers to act. More than three decades later, extended producer responsibility laws worldwide have evolved from that single national response into one of the most significant regulatory trends reshaping global manufacturing and retail. Europe remains the most mature region for these frameworks, with approximately 40 to 45 countries now operating established EPR schemes. The European Union’s Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation, which entered into force in February 2025 and applies fully from August 2026, replaced the previous directive with uniform, directly applicable requirements across all member states. The regulation requires packaging to meet EU recyclability performance criteria, sets recycled-content targets for plastic packaging starting in 2030, and restricts PFAS in food-contact packaging starting in August 2026. Extended producer responsibility laws worldwide increasingly extend beyond packaging alone. France’s framework, codified in its Environmental Code in 1992, now covers packaging, paper, textiles, electrical and electronic equipment, and batteries, with industrial and commercial packaging added to the scope in January 2025. This expansion reflects a broader pattern: once EPR infrastructure exists for one product category, governments frequently extend similar accountability to additional waste streams. In Asia, Japan’s Container and Packaging Recycling Law dates to 1997, obligating producers to fund recycling for designated packaging materials, while recent circular economy obligations have supplemented rather than replaced that core framework. South Korea operates what is widely considered one of the strictest EPR systems globally under its Resource Circulation Act, requiring companies to reduce packaging weight, improve recyclability, and submit to public disclosure of violators as a reputational enforcement mechanism alongside heavy fines. Extended Producer Responsibility laws worldwide increasingly rely on eco-modulated fees that reward recyclable, reusable, or sustainably designed packaging, creating market pressure for companies across Europe, Asia, and the Americas to redesign products proactively rather than simply absorbing compliance costs. Photo by Mikhail Nilov on Pexels. China’s approach folds extended producer responsibility obligations into its broader Law on Prevention and Control of Environmental Pollution by Solid Waste, expanding registration and recycling reporting requirements for both electronics and packaging sectors. India’s Plastic Waste Rules, first introduced in 2016 and amended in 2022, require producers, importers, and brand owners to register and take direct responsibility for collecting, recycling, or disposing of plastic packaging waste they introduce into the market. Extended producer responsibility laws worldwide show particularly rapid momentum across the Americas. In Canada, most provinces are fully transitioning to EPR models for packaging and printed paper, requiring registration with provincial programs, annual reporting by material type and weight, and payment of eco-modulated fees that vary by packaging performance and recyclability. Brazil’s National Policy on Solid Waste requires manufacturers, importers, distributors, and sellers to implement reverse-logistics systems that ensure packaging is reused or recycled rather than discarded. Chile’s Law 20.920 similarly requires producers of priority products to establish their own collection, recovery, and recycling schemes to meet government-set targets. In the United States, more than half a dozen states have already implemented EPR legislation, with additional states expected to follow as the model gains bipartisan traction. This state-by-state approach creates a patchwork of overlapping requirements that producers selling nationally must navigate simultaneously. Beyond mandatory frameworks, some nations have pursued voluntary or co-regulatory pathways as stepping stones toward fuller accountability. Australia’s National Packaging Targets, administered by the Australian Packaging Covenant Organization, aim for 100% of packaging to be recyclable, reusable, or compostable and operate through industry-led stewardship rather than direct government mandate. New Zealand has introduced voluntary EPR initiatives for packaging, with mandatory requirements expected as the voluntary phase matures. A common thread across extended producer responsibility laws worldwide is eco-modulated fee structures, financial penalties or incentives tied directly to how recyclable, reusable, or sustainably designed a product’s packaging is. This design creates market pressure encouraging companies to redesign packaging proactively rather than simply paying compliance costs passively, since better-designed packaging typically carries lower fees under most EPR schemes. For companies operating or distributing products internationally, this patchwork of national and regional requirements creates genuine compliance complexity. Registration requirements, reporting formats, fee structures, and penalty regimes vary significantly by country, even as the underlying principle that producers bear responsibility for their products’ end-of-life impact remains consistent across jurisdictions. As extended producer responsibility laws worldwide continue expanding into new product categories and new countries, the regulatory trajectory points firmly in one direction: toward holding manufacturers accountable not just for what they sell, but for what eventually becomes of it, transforming waste management from a public cost into a cost of doing business built directly into product design and corporate strategy. The post Extended Producer Responsibility Laws Worldwide Now Cover More Than 70 Countries appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.description: ΑΠΟ ΤΗΝ ΚΑΘΗΜΕΡΙΝΗ ΣΥΝΤΑΚΤΙΚΗ ΟΜΑΔΑ OPTIMIST Σε μια κλινική δοκιμή του 2023 σε 121 άτομα στο Ηνωμένο Βασίλειο, η χρήση μιας πρωτότυπης συσκευής καρπού μείωσε τη συχνότητα τικ κατά μέσο όρο 25 τοις εκατό. Η συσκευή καρπού του Tourette, που ονομάζεται Neupulse, προέκυψε από έρευνα στο Πανεπιστήμιο του Νότιγχαμ και τρία χρόνια μετά, οι άνθρωποι που τη χρησιμοποιούν περιγράφουν την επίδρασή της πολύ πιο ισχυρά.…
items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM In a 2023 clinical trial of 121 people in the UK, wearing a prototype wrist device reduced tic frequency by an average of 25 percent. The Tourette’s wrist device, called Neupulse , came out of research at the University of Nottingham, and three years on, the people using it describe its effect in far stronger terms than a one-in-four reduction would suggest. How a Tourette’s wrist device targets tics Rhythmic pulses to the median nerve Neupulse sends rhythmic electrical pulses into the median nerve, which runs through the wrist and into the hand. Trials have shown that this stimulation changes activity in the brain regions responsible for movement control, and that the rhythm of the pulses can lower both the frequency and the intensity of tics. The device was developed by the university and its spin-out company, Neurotherapeutics Ltd, which secured £1 million (about $1.3 million) in additional funding to bring it to market. Stephen Jackson, the Nottingham professor who has led the research, described the response from users as “a dream come true.” Some of the feedback he has received is very concrete. “We’ve had people saying they managed to get through their wedding vows without ticking,” he said. Others told the team they could move through an airport and board a flight without tics. Tourette’s syndrome in the UK Tourette’s syndrome is a neurodevelopmental condition, usually beginning in childhood, that causes involuntary sounds and movements known as tics. More than 300,000 people in the UK have it, according to the charity Tourettes Action , and there is no cure. The condition reached a wider audience in 2023 when singer Lewis Capaldi, who has Tourette’s, tried the device before a concert in Nottingham, and again through the film I Swear , a drama based on the life of Tourette’s campaigner John Davidson. Three users, three measurable changes Katie, 15: years of constant vocal tics Katie, from Hertfordshire, started having tics at age seven. Her snorting tic ran almost nonstop, to the point of leaving her with a sore throat that kept her in bed for two weeks, and it disrupted her sleep, her eating, and her school attendance. “It was constantly moving, constantly making sounds and then I was kind of getting looked at like, ‘why are you doing that?'” she said. Her mom, Julia, called it “heartbreaking” to watch. “You feel helpless. You feel you don’t know where to turn really,” she said. After reading about the Nottingham research, Julia brought Katie to try the device in December, before it went on sale. The effect was immediate, Katie said, and she became “really calm.” “It was absolutely life-changing. It was like the best day of my life,” she said. On the drive back to Hertfordshire, she “just cried the whole way home.” Ollie, 15: a different diagnosis, a similar response Ollie’s case extends the picture, because he does not have Tourette’s. Nearly two years ago he cracked his neck, and about 48 hours later the movement had become involuntary and constant. “It was incredibly sudden,” he said. He was later diagnosed with functional neurological disorder (FND), a condition that affects how the brain sends and receives signals. His father, Alex, said sleeping, eating and drinking all became “incredibly difficult.” Ollie stayed inside for about a month at one stage and missed six to seven months of school ahead of his GCSEs, the exams British students sit around age 16. He came close to telling his parents not to bother with the device. A few months ago, when he switched it on for the first time, he phoned home. “You could hear that he was crying on the telephone because it had worked and his neck movement had stopped,” Alex said. Ollie put it this way: “It’s like a light switch. I remember my hands were quite shaky when I was calling my parents because it’s like getting part of your life back.” Mylo, 17: from trial participant to owner Mylo, from Buckinghamshire, was 13 when he joined the 2023 trial. He recently received his own device as a gift and said the urge to suppress his facial tics went away “instantaneously.” “As soon as it comes on, I can feel it,” he said. “I feel different… I feel new almost, which is strange.” Why Neupulse is not yet an NHS treatment Wellness product versus medical device The device comes in two versions. Neupulse-C is sold as a consumer wellness product, and the university says “thousands” have been purchased. Neupulse-M is the version intended for marketing as a medical treatment for tics and Tourette’s syndrome, and it is still working through regulatory approval. That distinction determines whether the National Health Service can offer it. The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) has identified the technology as “promising” but asked for more evidence of long-term benefit. In 2025, it said its committee would meet again to assess the device’s clinical and cost-effectiveness. “They were unable to recommend it for use in the NHS until we have the regulatory approval,” Jackson said. “That’s something we’re working towards.” He hopes to see the Tourette’s wrist device available through the NHS “in the next year or so.” Early reports from the Tourette’s community Emma McNally, CEO of Tourettes Action , said the users she has spoken with have given the device “nothing but praise.” “Some people have said it’s helped them to go to places that they’ve not been for a long time, such as the cinema or a library,” she said. Others told her it helped them come out of a tic attack and feel more relaxed. Wrist stimulation beyond Tourette’s syndrome The Nottingham team is now testing the same approach on other conditions. Early trials have examined whether the pulses can reduce tremors in people with Parkinson’s , and Jackson said the university plans a UK-wide clinical trial covering anxiety and obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD). The next milestone is regulatory, since medical approval for Neupulse-M would open the door to NICE guidance and NHS prescriptions, and the trials that follow will show whether a signal sent through the wrist can shape movement and mood in conditions well beyond tics. items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM You know that feeling when it’s two in the afternoon, and you can’t quite account for where the morning went? Not because you weren’t doing things, but because the busyness didn’t add up to anything you can point to. It’s demoralizing in a specific way, and it has surprisingly little to do with how early your alarm went off. Time management experts Melinda Rathkopf, M.D., M.B.A. , and Julie Morgenstern , the author of multiple bestselling books on productivity, say most of what shapes your morning was set in motion the night before, and the solution is usually far simpler than the elaborate routines you’ve seen floating around online. Start the night before Where do both experts begin? The evening before. When you make decisions about tomorrow before you go to sleep, you take some of the friction out of the morning itself. “Preplanning the day ahead and making decisions ahead of time makes the rest of your day potentially calmer and less stressful,” says Rathkopf. “Set yourself up by knowing what’s coming.” Transition time is one of the things that tends to get left out when people plan their days. It’s easy to schedule back-to-back tasks and forget that moving between them really does take time. Build that in the night before and the morning feels a lot less like you’re already behind before you’ve started. This extends to sleep, too. Rathkopf recommends starting with how much sleep you genuinely need to feel refreshed, then working backward from your wake time to set a consistent bedtime. “ Sleep is so vital to daily functioning and brain health,” she says. Most people schedule everything else first and try to fit sleep in around it. She suggests reversing that. Put the phone away before bed and after waking up If there’s one habit both experts come back to, it’s keeping your phone out of your first and last hour of each day. Morgenstern is direct about it. “The number one thing that can boost morning productivity has to do with screen time ,” she says. “We should not be on our devices an hour before bed, and we should not be on our devices for our first hour of the morning.” Checking your phone first thing does more than eat up time. It pulls you into a reactive state before you’ve had a chance to figure out your own priorities for the day. “The phone can be a useful tool, but it’s designed to keep us on there,” Morgenstern says. “Think of it like sugar — you have to really manage your consumption, and take charge. It’s the key to morning productivity, engagement, your relationships, everything.” She recommends replacing that screen time with something restorative: reading, getting outside, or having a conversation with someone. The goal isn’t deprivation; it’s starting the day on your own terms instead of somebody else’s notifications. Keep your routine simple One persistent myth about productive mornings is that they require an elaborate ritual. If you’ve ever felt vaguely inadequate watching someone describe their two-hour routine involving cold plunges , journaling, and a complicated smoothie, you’re not alone. Those routines often backfire. “It can make you stressed out — ‘Oh god, I didn’t meditate long enough!'” Morgenstern says. “Add three to four elements maximum for a morning routine. Otherwise, you’re habituating to something that’s unsustainable.” Find the small handful of things that reliably start your morning feeling calm and grounded, and stick with those. If you’re getting ready alongside young children, Morgenstern suggests completing your own routine before they’re up, then putting some thought into making their mornings smoother too. Laying out clothes or choosing breakfast the night before can take a surprising amount of stress out of a weekday morning. Train your brain with predictability Your brain is a creature of habit in the most useful sense. “Our brains love predictability,” says Rathkopf. “When you have a predictable routine, you’re reducing your stress and cognitive load.” When your morning follows a consistent pattern, you spend less mental energy on logistics and more on the work itself, which sounds obvious until you notice how rarely most mornings feel that way in practice. Morgenstern describes building a regular block for deep thinking as a kind of training for your brain: “If you have a predictable head-down time, your brain gets acclimated to it — it’s 10:30, that’s when we do our deep thinking. I’ve never seen anyone build proactive work with an erratic schedule.” For creative work especially, consistency turns out to matter more than inspiration. Start with the work that matters most A lot of mornings get swallowed by emails, messages, and reactive tasks before you ever reach work that needs your purest attention. “The number one difficulty people have is that the day starts off all reactive, and they can’t get to proactive work,” Morgenstern says. Her suggestion is to start with the most important thing on your list, the one that needs your freshest thinking. Even if everything else gets away from you after that, you’ve done something that mattered. “Even if you only get that one thing done, you’ll feel the greatest sense of relief that you’ve done your job,” she says. If your workplace opens with a morning meeting, Morgenstern recommends blocking off a half hour to an hour right after it for focused work, to address anything that came out of the meeting before settling into your main task. Better yet, see if you can get your whole team to protect the first hour of the day. Build in small moments of recovery Self-care doesn’t need to be a whole thing. What Morgenstern recommends is more modest: short pauses woven throughout the day, especially during your busiest stretches. “Add microbursts of self-care in your day — five to 20-minute activities that recharge you,” she says. A short walk, some music on your commute, ten minutes with a book. Small enough to fit into almost any day, and consistent enough to keep you from burning out by three in the afternoon. “The harder you’re working, the harder you have to recover,” she says. Stopping feels like the last thing you can afford when you’re slammed, but that’s usually when it matters most. Give yourself room to change, and to have off days Both experts caution against treating your morning routine as something fixed. Life changes, seasons change, your circumstances shift, and what works at one stage may not work at another. “You may need to change it based on other obligations, at different stages of your life, or even in different seasons,” says Rathkopf. And when a morning doesn’t come together the way you hoped, she has one more piece of advice: don’t be hard on yourself about it. “Everybody’s different, and what you’re seeing in posts is someone else’s best versions and best days,” Rathkopf says. “They have those not-so-perfect days, too.” A morning routine isn’t something you get right once. It’s something you keep adjusting until it fits. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . The post 8 simple habits time management experts say build a better morning first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .
